categories.name: Compute
categories.blurb: Virtual machines and the options that change their price, placement, and lifecycle.
categories.intro: Compute questions ask which VM-based platform fits the workload. Then they ask you to choose the machine type, provisioning model, tenancy, and group design.

decide.if: The workload needs OS, kernel, or disk control, or a quick lift-and-shift of a VM
decide.why: You choose the OS, machine type, and disks, and you control the VM lifecycle.

decide.if: A VM tier must keep serving through a zone failure and scale with load
decide.why: A regional MIG spreads VMs across zones and adds autohealing and autoscaling.

decide.if: Fault-tolerant batch work that retries or checkpoints, at the lowest price
decide.why: Spot VMs cost up to 91% less, but Compute Engine can preempt them at any time.

decide.if: Many independent, restartable tasks, with no job scheduler or VMs to manage
decide.why: Batch queues the jobs and creates the VMs, and Spot VMs cut the cost.

decide.if: BYOL licenses count physical cores, or rules require physical isolation from other customers
decide.why: Sole-tenant nodes are physical servers that host only your project's VMs.

decide.if: A VMware estate must leave the data center fast, with the same tools and runbooks
decide.why: It runs vSphere, vCenter, vSAN, NSX, and HCX, so operations do not change.

decide.if: Specialized software, such as Oracle, needs dedicated servers, a third-party hypervisor, or low-level server access
decide.why: It gives dedicated bare-metal servers under BYOL, and you manage the OS and everything above it.

categories.name: Containers and serverless
categories.blurb: Where to run containers and code without managing VMs.
categories.intro: These questions ask where containers and code run with the least operational work. The deciding facts are a Kubernetes dependency, run time, event triggers, and node control.

decide.if: Stateless HTTP container, spiky traffic, small team, no Kubernetes dependency
decide.why: Google recommends serverless first unless you need Kubernetes.

decide.if: Containerized batch runs for hours, splits into parallel parts, and serves no requests
decide.why: A Cloud Run job task can run up to 168 hours, but a request stops at 60 minutes.

decide.if: Single-purpose code must react to an event, such as a file upload or a new BigQuery row
decide.why: Event-driven functions receive events through Eventarc triggers.

decide.if: The app ships as a Helm chart, uses custom resources, or calls the Kubernetes API
decide.why: Cloud Run does not support Kubernetes, and Autopilot is the recommended GKE mode.

decide.if: The workload needs privileged Pods or direct control of nodes
decide.why: Autopilot does not allow privileged Pods, so use GKE Standard and manage the node pools.

decide.if: Cloud and on-premises clusters must be managed together, or share one global entry point
decide.why: A fleet groups clusters, including clusters outside Google Cloud, so you manage them together.

decide.if: A new web application is proposed on App Engine
decide.why: Google recommends Cloud Run instead of App Engine for new projects.

categories.name: Storage
categories.blurb: Object, block, and file storage, and backup.
categories.intro: Storage questions ask you to pick the storage type from the access method first. Then you pick the product and tier that meet the protocol, availability, and recovery needs.

decide.if: Unstructured files or media of any size, read from anywhere, with unlimited growth
decide.why: Cloud Storage has no capacity limit, and you pick the class from access frequency.

decide.if: A VM disk needs IOPS and throughput set separately from its size
decide.why: Hyperdisk performance is independent of the provisioned capacity.

decide.if: Many VMs share files over NFS, and the share must survive a zone outage
decide.why: The Filestore Regional tier is built for resilience to zone outages.

decide.if: Windows servers need SMB file shares
decide.why: Filestore serves NFS, not SMB, and NetApp Volumes supports SMB.

decide.if: Thousands of clients read and write the same files in parallel, for HPC or AI checkpoints
decide.why: Google names Managed Lustre as the parallel file system for AI, ML, and HPC.

decide.if: Training code reads a bucket through a file path and rereads data that rarely changes
decide.why: FUSE mounts the bucket, and Rapid Cache serves repeated reads from a zonal SSD cache.

decide.if: Backups must stay undeletable for a set period, even by a project owner
decide.why: A backup vault with locked enforced retention keeps backups immutable and indelible.

categories.name: Databases
categories.blurb: Managed relational, NoSQL, and in-memory databases.
categories.intro: Database questions ask you to match the data model and workload to a product. Then you check scale, consistency, global reach, and operational overhead.

decide.if: Existing MySQL, PostgreSQL, or SQL Server app in one region, moving to a managed service
decide.why: Cloud SQL is managed MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server for general-purpose OLTP.

decide.if: A PostgreSQL app needs analytics on live transactional data, with no rewrite and no pipeline
decide.why: The AlloyDB columnar engine runs analytical queries on live transactional data.

decide.if: Global users, relational schema, strongly consistent writes, and survival of a region outage
decide.why: Spanner scales horizontally, and multi-region configurations have a 99.999% SLA.

decide.if: Time-series or IoT data at very high throughput, read by key
decide.why: Bigtable serves large single-keyed data with low latency and high throughput.

decide.if: Mobile or web app with document data, offline sync, and no capacity planning
decide.why: Firestore is serverless, and its client libraries support offline edits and real-time updates.

decide.if: Sessions or cache data need sub-millisecond access outside the app servers
decide.why: Memorystore keeps data in memory, with replicas across zones.

decide.if: Interactive SQL analytics over large datasets (OLAP)
decide.why: Google recommends BigQuery for interactive OLAP queries, not the serving databases.

categories.name: Data analytics and pipelines
categories.blurb: Warehousing, streaming, batch processing, orchestration, and catalogs.
categories.intro: Data questions give a source, a latency need, team skills, and existing code. You pick the managed ingestion, processing, and orchestration services with the least operations work that still meet every requirement.

decide.if: Messages already in Pub/Sub must land in BigQuery unchanged, with the least overhead
decide.why: A BigQuery subscription writes messages to a table with no subscriber code and no Dataflow job.

decide.if: A stream needs event-time windows, aggregation across messages, or late-data handling
decide.why: Dataflow uses windows, watermarks, and triggers, with exactly-once processing by default.

decide.if: Existing Spark or Hadoop jobs must move with the same code
decide.why: Managed Spark runs the code as is, while Dataflow would need a rewrite in Apache Beam.

decide.if: Existing applications depend on Kafka, or the workload is a new streaming design
decide.why: Google recommends Managed Kafka for existing Kafka workloads and Pub/Sub for new ones.

decide.if: Analysts need operational tables in BigQuery within minutes, and the source database stays primary
decide.why: Datastream is serverless CDC into BigQuery, while Database Migration Service moves the primary.

decide.if: Batch ETL steps across BigQuery, Dataflow, and Spark run as Python DAGs with dependencies and backfills
decide.why: Managed Airflow orchestrates data pipelines, while Workflows chains low-latency HTTP services.

decide.if: Analysts cannot find trusted data or see where it came from across many datasets and buckets
decide.why: Knowledge Catalog adds discovery, data quality scans, and lineage without copying the data.

categories.name: Application integration and APIs
categories.blurb: Events, orchestration, task queues, scheduling, and API management.
categories.intro: Integration questions give one hard constraint, such as a partner rate limit, a failure that must not spread, or an approval. You pick the interaction style first, then the queue, orchestrator, integration platform, or API layer that meets it.

decide.if: One event must reach several consumers that fail and recover on their own
decide.why: Pub/Sub delivers each message to every subscription, while Cloud Tasks has one handler per task.

decide.if: Calls to one partner API must stay under its rate limit, with retries, and the caller must not wait
decide.why: The sender controls the dispatch rate and retries on a Cloud Tasks queue.

decide.if: A process inside one team's domain needs one status view and a wait of days for a human decision
decide.why: Workflows orchestrates the services, holds state, and waits on a callback with no polling.

decide.if: Work must start when something happens, such as a file upload or new rows, not at fixed times
decide.why: An Eventarc trigger reacts to each event, while a Cloud Scheduler job runs even when nothing changed.

decide.if: Business analysts connect Salesforce, ServiceNow, or SFTP partners with data mapping and little code
decide.why: Application Integration is an iPaaS with prebuilt connectors and a drag-and-drop editor.

decide.if: Partners need self-service app registration, a developer portal, usage tiers, or monetization
decide.why: Apigee has API products, a portal, and monetization, which API Gateway lacks.

decide.if: Serverless backends need a managed, pay-per-call gateway for project-level APIs with no portal
decide.why: Google suggests API Gateway for serverless projects without partner, scale, or governance needs.

categories.name: Networking and connectivity
categories.blurb: VPC design, private access, load balancing, DNS, and hybrid links.
categories.intro: The exam asks how to connect VPC networks, sites, and clouds, and how workloads reach APIs and services privately. It also asks which load balancer and hybrid link fit the protocol, scope, cost, and SLA.

decide.if: Many projects in one organization; a central team must control all subnets, routes, and firewall rules
decide.why: Shared VPC keeps one network in a host project, but host and service projects must share one organization.

decide.if: Many VPC networks, some in another organization, must reach each other and be managed from one place
decide.why: NCC VPC spokes are transitive and can cross organizations; peering is not transitive.

decide.if: A consumer needs one service from a producer, with overlapping IP ranges or in another organization
decide.why: PSC uses NAT, so no IP coordination is needed, and it exposes one service, not a network.

decide.if: VMs without external IP addresses must reach Google APIs, and internet access is forbidden
decide.why: Private Google Access reaches only Google APIs and services; Cloud NAT would open the internet.

decide.if: VMs without external IP addresses must call an internet API from fixed source addresses
decide.why: Public NAT with manually assigned NAT IP addresses gives a partner a stable allowlist.

decide.if: Hybrid link with high throughput that must stay off the public internet
decide.why: Google positions Cloud Interconnect for higher throughput and Cloud VPN for lower bandwidth or cost.

decide.if: HTTP(S) users in many countries need low latency and one public IP address
decide.why: The global external Application Load Balancer gives one anycast IP address for backends in many regions and ends TLS close to users.

categories.name: Network security
categories.blurb: Controls that filter, inspect, or fence traffic.
categories.intro: The exam asks which control fits the traffic layer: VM firewall, load balancer WAF, outbound web proxy, or API perimeter. It also tests whether the requirement is to block a threat or only detect it.

decide.if: Allow or deny VM traffic by IP range, port, protocol, or workload identity
decide.why: Cloud NGFW rules apply at each VM; Cloud Armor works at load balancers and public IP addresses.

decide.if: Block exploits and command-and-control traffic inline, also between tiers inside the VPC network
decide.why: Cloud NGFW Enterprise intrusion prevention blocks inline; Cloud IDS only detects and alerts.

decide.if: Detect threats in a copy of the traffic for PCI or HIPAA, with alerts only
decide.why: Cloud IDS inspects mirrored traffic and alerts without changing the traffic path.

decide.if: Public web app needs WAF rules, per-client rate limits, or geography blocks
decide.why: Cloud Armor security policies attach to load balancer backend services.

decide.if: Outbound HTTP(S) allowed only for one service account to one host and URL path, with a log of each request
decide.why: Secure Web Proxy denies by default, matches source identity and URL path, and logs each request.

decide.if: Stop copies of BigQuery or Cloud Storage data out of the company, even with valid credentials
decide.why: A service perimeter blocks API requests that cross it, even when IAM allows them.

decide.if: Network rules for the whole organization that no project can override
decide.why: A hierarchical firewall policy sits on the organization or a folder, and lower levels cannot override it.

categories.name: Identity and access
categories.blurb: Who can do what, and how people and workloads sign in.
categories.intro: Identity questions ask who gets access, at which level of the hierarchy, and with which credential. They also test guardrails that apply to everyone, including project owners.

decide.if: A group needs a role in every current and future project under one folder
decide.why: A folder grant is inherited by every project in the folder, including new ones.

decide.if: One group must lose one inherited permission in one project, and all other access must stay the same
decide.why: Allow policies are a union, so only a deny policy removes an inherited permission.

decide.if: A configuration rule must hold for everyone, including project owners, in current and future projects
decide.why: An organization policy restricts what anyone can configure; roles only decide who can act.

decide.if: Code must act as a service account, and service account keys are forbidden
decide.why: External workloads federate their own credentials; people and local tests impersonate with Token Creator.

decide.if: Employees sign in with Active Directory credentials, and deletions in Active Directory must reach Google Cloud
decide.why: GCDS syncs users and groups one way, and SAML SSO keeps Active Directory in charge of passwords.

decide.if: Admins need SSH to VMs with no external IP address, and no bastion host or VPN
decide.why: IAP TCP forwarding opens the tunnel, and OS Login ties each login to IAM roles.

decide.if: Access is allowed only from company-managed devices
decide.why: IAP enforces the access level, and device attributes in access levels need Chrome Enterprise Premium.

categories.name: Data protection and compliance
categories.blurb: Keys, secrets, sensitive data, supply chain, and regulated workloads.
categories.intro: Security questions ask which control meets a named requirement: key control, key location, secrets, sensitive data, image trust, residency, or audit evidence. The wrong answers are usually real controls that protect something else.

decide.if: You must control, rotate, or disable the keys that protect your data
decide.why: Default encryption gives no key control, and CMEK puts your Cloud KMS key in charge.

decide.if: Keys must be in FIPS 140-2 Level 3 hardware, or key material must stay outside Google
decide.why: Hardware protection points to Cloud HSM; keys held outside Google point to Cloud EKM.

decide.if: A build or app needs a password or API token at runtime
decide.why: Secret Manager returns the value to authorized identities; Cloud KMS never returns key material.

decide.if: A chatbot must block prompt injection, or keep personal data out of responses and logs
decide.why: Model Armor screens prompts and responses; Sensitive Data Protection finds and de-identifies personal data.

decide.if: Only approved images, or images that Cloud Build built, may deploy to GKE or Cloud Run
decide.why: Binary Authorization blocks at deploy time; Artifact Analysis scanning only reports.

decide.if: EU-only data locations and EU-based support staff, with predefined controls
decide.why: A control package on a folder sets both the location and the support controls.

decide.if: An auditor asks who did something: your own users, or Google personnel
decide.why: Cloud Audit Logs record your principals; Access Transparency records Google personnel.

categories.name: AI and ML
categories.blurb: Models, agents, pre-trained APIs, ML pipelines, and accelerators.
categories.intro: Most questions ask how far to climb the build-versus-buy ladder: pre-trained API, Gemini prompt, grounding, tuning, or custom training. Others ask which product fits employees, customers, or developers, and how to buy accelerator capacity.

decide.if: One common, narrow task, such as image labels, text moderation, transcription, or translation, with no training
decide.why: A pre-trained API is the lowest-effort rung when one feature matches the task exactly.

decide.if: The task mixes text, images, audio, or video, or the output must follow your own schema
decide.why: One multimodal prompt with a response schema replaces a chain of APIs and mapping code.

decide.if: A Gemini app must answer from private documents that change often, with sources
decide.why: Grounding adds current facts at request time; tuning teaches skills, not facts.

decide.if: Data is in BigQuery, analysts know only SQL, and the data must not move
decide.why: BigQuery ML creates models and runs predictions inside the warehouse with SQL.

decide.if: Employees need one permissions-aware search and assistant across SharePoint, Confluence, and Jira
decide.why: Prebuilt connectors and permission-aware results need no custom RAG build.

decide.if: A customer-facing voice or chat agent that non-developers build and change
decide.why: CX Agent Studio is minimal-code; ADK on Agent Runtime fits developers who write code.

decide.if: GPU training needs capacity: a flexible start for up to 7 days, or a fixed date for 1 to 90 days
decide.why: Flex-start fits the flexible short job; a future reservation in calendar mode fits the fixed date.

categories.name: Developer tools, CI/CD, and IaC
categories.blurb: Build, deploy, provision, and work with Google Cloud from code.
categories.intro: The exam asks you to pick the tool for each delivery stage: build, artifacts, release promotion, and infrastructure as code. It also tests the Google-recommended identity, state, and review practices around those tools.

decide.if: Code must be built and tested on each push or pull request, and vulnerable images must fail the build
decide.why: Cloud Build runs the CI steps, and On-Demand Scanning in the pipeline can fail the build.

decide.if: One release must move through dev, staging, and prod in order, with approvals, a canary, or a change freeze
decide.why: Cloud Deploy owns the promotion sequence, target approvals, canary phases, and deploy policies.

decide.if: Builds stop when Docker Hub or PyPI is down, or a public package can shadow a private one
decide.why: Remote repositories cache upstream packages, and a virtual repository puts the private repository first.

decide.if: A team wants Google to run Terraform and keep the state, or must leave Deployment Manager
decide.why: Infrastructure Manager runs Terraform and stores state per revision, and DM Convert feeds it.

decide.if: Kubernetes GitOps teams declare cloud resources as manifests, with drift reverted and policy enforced
decide.why: Config Controller hosts Config Connector together with Config Sync and Policy Controller.

decide.if: Developers self-deploy approved application templates, and each application must appear in App Hub
decide.why: Application Design Center deploys the templates, and App Hub registers each deployed application.

decide.if: Local code must run with a service account's permissions, and key creation is blocked
decide.why: Impersonation through the ADC login gives client libraries short-lived credentials without a key.

categories.name: Operations, observability, and support
categories.blurb: Monitoring, logging, troubleshooting, patching, and support plans.
categories.intro: The exam asks which tool answers an observability question, and how to centralize metrics and logs across projects. It also tests symptom-based alerting, support services, case priority, and where to check for Google Cloud incidents.

decide.if: One SRE team needs dashboards and alerting policies across many projects
decide.why: A metrics scope in a project without resources charts and alerts on all monitored projects.

decide.if: Alert when customers cannot complete a checkout, before anyone reports it
decide.why: A synthetic monitor runs a scripted user journey, while an uptime check tests one endpoint.

decide.if: Logs from many projects must stay in one place for years
decide.why: An aggregated sink routes logs from a folder or organization to a central bucket.

decide.if: Count or group log entries with SQL, including entries that are already stored
decide.why: Observability Analytics queries stored logs, and new sinks or log-based metrics are not retroactive.

decide.if: CPU use rose after a release, but latency and error rates did not change
decide.why: Cloud Profiler maps CPU and memory use to code, and Cloud Trace measures latency.

decide.if: Critical production cases need a 15-minute first response and a named Google contact
decide.why: Only Premium Support has a 15-minute P1 target and includes a Technical Account Manager.

decide.if: The public status page is green, but resources in one zone fail
decide.why: Google communicates limited-scope incidents only through Personalized Service Health.

categories.name: Migration
categories.blurb: Assess, move, and transfer VMs, databases, and data.
categories.intro: Migration questions give a source, a target, and a constraint such as downtime, bandwidth, or team skills. You pick the assessment tool, the migration type, and the tool that matches the source and the target.

decide.if: Discover assets, group them by application, and estimate TCO before the move
decide.why: Migration Center discovers and groups assets and builds TCO reports from migration preferences.

decide.if: Rehost VMs from vSphere, AWS, or Azure on Compute Engine with a short cutover
decide.why: It replicates disks while the source runs and supports test clones before cutover.

decide.if: VMware VMs must leave the data center fast, and operations must keep vCenter, NSX, and VMware runbooks
decide.why: VMware Engine includes HCX and keeps the VMs unchanged, while Migrate to Virtual Machines converts them.

decide.if: MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, or Oracle must move to Cloud SQL or AlloyDB with minimal downtime
decide.why: A continuous migration replicates changes until you promote the target.

decide.if: Data must reach Cloud Storage from another cloud, or more than 1 TB from on-premises over enough bandwidth
decide.why: Storage Transfer Service runs managed, incremental transfers and can stay under a bandwidth limit.

decide.if: An online upload would take more than one week, or more bandwidth cannot arrive before the deadline
decide.why: You copy the data to a shipped appliance, and Google uploads it to Cloud Storage.

decide.if: A Teradata or other data warehouse moves to BigQuery, with SQL translation and a copy of schema and data
decide.why: BigQuery Migration Service translates the SQL, and BigQuery Data Transfer Service copies schema and data.

categories.name: Cost management
categories.intro: Cost questions give a spend pattern and a risk, and ask which cost lever fits. You choose among discounts, reservations, budgets, and quotas, and you must know what each one does not do.

decide.if: Steady usage of one machine series in one region for the whole term
decide.why: A resource-based commitment discounts stable usage in a known region and machine series.

decide.if: Steady hourly spend that moves across regions, machine series, GKE, or Cloud Run
decide.why: A compute flexible commitment follows eligible spend across the billing account.

decide.if: VMs must be able to start in a specific zone, for DR or a planned event
decide.why: Only a reservation holds zonal capacity. Quotas and commitments do not.

decide.if: A stable fleet needs both the lowest price and assured capacity in one zone
decide.why: Buy a resource-based commitment for the discount, and attach a reservation for the capacity.

decide.if: Finance wants cost by team and environment inside shared projects, down to single resources, in SQL
decide.why: Resource labels flow into billing data, and the detailed usage cost export adds resource-level cost.

decide.if: An automatic action must run when a project exceeds its budget
decide.why: An alerts-only budget only notifies, so send its notifications to Pub/Sub and let a function act.

decide.if: Each user or project needs a hard limit on consumption, such as daily BigQuery bytes per analyst
decide.why: A quota limits usage, not money, and a query over a custom quota does not run.

services.name: Compute Engine
services.what: Compute Engine runs virtual machines. You choose the OS, machine type, disks, and GPUs, and you operate and patch the OS.
cues: The company has only compiled binaries, and the workload must be rehosted fast with minimal changes.
The workload needs OS, kernel, or disk control, or it is a lift-and-shift of a VM.
Software is licensed per vCPU, and no predefined machine type matches the tested vCPU and memory.
The workload needs a specific machine shape, such as memory-optimized VMs for SAP HANA.
traps: Turning off vCPUs in the guest OS does not cut per-vCPU license cost, so use a custom machine type.
Shielded VM protects boot integrity, not data in memory, which needs Confidential VM.

confused.tell: A stateless HTTP container goes to Cloud Run, while Compute Engine fits when you need OS control.
A rehost with no source code goes to Compute Engine VMs, because a refactor into containers needs code changes.
Migrate to Virtual Machines converts VMs to Compute Engine and changes the tools, while VMware Engine keeps vCenter and NSX.

docs.title: Machine families resource and comparison guide

services.name: Managed instance groups (MIGs)
services.what: A managed instance group (MIG) runs identical VMs from one instance template. It adds autohealing, autoscaling, and rolling updates, and a regional MIG spreads VMs across zones.
cues: A VM tier must keep serving users if one zone fails.
A web tier must carry full peak load after a zone loss, without waiting for new VMs.
VMs whose application freezes or crashes must be recreated automatically.
A new instance template must roll out with no loss of serving capacity.
traps: Extra VMs in the same zone do not help, because a zonal MIG stops when its zone fails.
Predictive autoscaling learns daily and weekly cycles, so a one-time sale needs a scaling schedule instead.

confused.tell: To autoscale, move sessions to Memorystore, because a stateful MIG keeps disks but cannot autoscale.
A MIG needs templates, images, health checks, and OS patching, while Cloud Run avoids that work for stateless containers.
Kubernetes installed on MIG VMs is self-managed, while GKE Autopilot manages the control plane, upgrades, and nodes.

services.name: Spot VMs
services.what: Spot VMs are Compute Engine VMs with discounts of up to 91%. Compute Engine can preempt them at any time, and no SLA covers them.
cues: A transcoding, rendering, or simulation job retries failed parts or restarts from checkpoints.
The company wants the lowest compute cost for fault-tolerant batch work.
Tasks run for more than 24 hours and must not stop at a fixed runtime limit.
traps: Preemptible VMs always stop after 24 hours, so pick Spot VMs for new designs.
Spot VMs do not fit a stateful database or a job that cannot restart.

confused.tell: Flex-start VMs are not preempted and run up to seven days, while Spot VMs can stop at any time.
Commitments fit steady all-day use, a nightly retrying batch fits Spot, and flexible CUDs do not cover Spot VMs.
A reservation assures capacity for standard VMs, but reservations cannot supply Spot VMs.

services.name: Sole-tenant nodes
services.what: Sole-tenant nodes are physical servers that host only your project's VMs. You pay for the whole node plus a sole-tenancy premium.
cues: The company brings Windows Server licenses that are licensed per physical core and need dedicated hardware.
A finance or healthcare rule requires physical separation from other customers' VMs.
Per-core licenses require VMs to stay on a fixed set of physical servers during host maintenance.
traps: SQL Server with License Mobility on an on-demand Windows Server image, and RHEL or SLES BYOS, do not need sole-tenant nodes.
The default host maintenance policy lets VMs move to any server, so it does not suit per-core licenses.

confused.tell: A per-vCPU license needs only a custom machine type, so sole-tenant nodes add cost without benefit.
Sole-tenant nodes isolate hardware, but they do not encrypt memory or verify boot components.

services.name: Batch
services.what: Batch schedules, queues, and runs batch jobs on Compute Engine VMs that it creates and deletes for you. Batch itself has no additional cost.
cues: A simulation splits into many independent tasks that can restart from the beginning.
The team does not want to run a job scheduler or provision VMs itself.
HPC, ML, or data-processing jobs need queuing and VM provisioning at scale.
traps: Jobs use the Compute Engine default service account unless you choose one, and it has the Editor role by default.

confused.tell: A MIG of Spot VMs leaves queuing and restarts to the team, while Batch queues jobs and retries tasks.
Containerized batch that ends within 7 days fits a Cloud Run job, while large HPC jobs on VMs fit Batch.

services.name: Google Cloud VMware Engine
services.what: Google Cloud VMware Engine runs vSphere, vCenter, vSAN, NSX, and HCX on dedicated bare metal in Google Cloud. Teams keep their VMware tools, skills, and processes.
cues: Hundreds of vSphere VMs must leave a data center within months, with no change to runbooks.
Operators want to keep vCenter and NSX policies, and some VMs must move with no downtime.
Compute Engine VMs must reach VMware VMs in a private cloud over internal IP addresses.
traps: A Standard VMware Engine network connects to a VPC network through VPC Network Peering, not private services access.
You cannot change the vSphere/vSAN subnets range later without deleting the private cloud.

confused.tell: Migrate to Virtual Machines adapts VMs to Compute Engine and changes the tools, while HCX moves VMware VMs unchanged.
VMware Engine runs VMware in Google Cloud locations, while Distributed Cloud runs GKE on your own servers.
Migrate to Containers is a modernization project, which does not fit a fast exit with the same operations.

services.name: Bare Metal Solution
services.what: Bare Metal Solution gives you dedicated bare-metal servers for specialized workloads, such as Oracle, under a bring-your-own-license model. You manage the OS, database, backups, patches, and licenses.
cues: Software needs a third-party hypervisor or low-level server access.
An Oracle workload needs dedicated servers, and the company brings its own licenses.
traps: Bare Metal Solution is not a managed database, because you run the OS and the database yourself.
For most Oracle deployments, Google positions Oracle Database@Google Cloud as the more integrated option.

confused.tell: Compute Engine bare metal instances (-metal machine types) are not related to Bare Metal Solution.

services.aws: Amazon RDS for Oracle (loose match, because Bare Metal Solution is not a managed database)

services.name: Cloud Run
services.what: Cloud Run is a serverless platform that runs containers as services, jobs, and worker pools. Services scale to zero by default and bill per use.
cues: A stateless containerized API has spiky traffic, and a small team has no Kubernetes skills or need.
A nightly containerized process runs for hours, splits into parallel parts, and serves no HTTP requests.
A small model must serve bursty traffic on a GPU, with no cost when idle and no reservation.
A pull-based consumer, such as Pub/Sub pull or Kafka, runs always on with no HTTP endpoint.
traps: A service request stops at 60 minutes, so multi-hour work belongs in a Cloud Run job.
Cloud Run never routes traffic to another region, so deploy to several regions behind a load balancer.

confused.tell: Pick GKE Autopilot when the app needs Helm, custom resources, or the Kubernetes API, which Cloud Run does not support.
A function is a Cloud Run service built from source, so pick a service when you build the image.
App Engine is the older platform, and Google recommends Cloud Run for new projects.

services.name: Cloud Run functions
services.what: Cloud Run functions are Cloud Run services that Cloud Run builds from your source code. They fit single-purpose, event-driven code, and event-driven functions use Eventarc triggers.
cues: A pipeline run must start soon after new rows land in a BigQuery table, without polling.
Code must run when a file lands in Cloud Storage or a message arrives on Pub/Sub.
A budget alert on Pub/Sub must stop VMs automatically but keep the stored data.
traps: Do not design around 1st gen limits, because current HTTP functions run up to 60 minutes with 1,000 concurrent requests per instance.
Use functions as event-driven glue for ML workflows, not as the place to train models.

confused.tell: Chained functions have no central view of retries or dependencies, so cross-system workflows go to Managed Service for Apache Airflow.
Functions mean custom mapping and retry code, while Application Integration gives prebuilt connectors and built-in error handling.
Choose a function for small event-driven code from source, and a service when you build the container image.

services.name: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)
services.what: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) runs managed Kubernetes clusters. Autopilot is the recommended mode, where GKE manages the nodes, scaling, and security defaults.
cues: A vendor app ships as a Helm chart with an operator that calls the Kubernetes API.
The team runs a self-managed Kubernetes cluster on VMs and wants to stop patching and upgrading it.
The workload needs Kubernetes volumes, Pods that run for days, network policies, or RBAC multi-tenancy.
The workload needs privileged Pods or direct node control, which points to GKE Standard.
traps: GKE Standard is not the default answer, so pick it only for privileged Pods or node-level control.
A zonal Standard cluster has one control plane and a lower SLA, so use a regional cluster for production.

confused.tell: A stateless API with no Kubernetes dependency goes to Cloud Run, which has less operational overhead than Autopilot.
One cluster is plain GKE, while managing many clusters, including on-premises ones, needs a fleet.
An ADK agent with no clusters to operate goes to Agent Runtime, not a GKE Deployment.

services.name: GKE Enterprise, fleets, and Google Distributed Cloud
patterns: (?i)registered to a fleet|\bone fleet\b|\ba fleet\b(?! of)|fleet host|fleet membership|multi-cluster Gateway|Cloud Service Mesh|Config Sync
services.what: A fleet is a logical group of Kubernetes clusters, including clusters outside Google Cloud, that you manage together. Google Distributed Cloud runs GKE clusters on your own servers.
cues: Operators must manage on-premises and cloud Kubernetes clusters together from Google Cloud.
Containers must run directly on existing physical servers, with no hypervisor layer.
Many clusters need the same configuration from Git, and noncompliant changes must be blocked.
Players need one global entry point that routes to the closest healthy cluster.
traps: There is no separate GKE Enterprise edition to choose, because GKE is now one offering without editions or tiers.
Do not mix environments in one fleet, because Google recommends clusters from only one environment per fleet.

confused.tell: VMware Engine runs the VMware platform in Google Cloud locations, while Distributed Cloud runs GKE on your own servers.
DNS geolocation routing gives players two regional IP addresses, while a multi-cluster Gateway gives one global entry point.

services.name: App Engine
services.what: App Engine is an older serverless platform with standard (sandbox) and flexible (containers on VMs) environments. Google recommends Cloud Run for new projects.
cues: The scenario already runs an app on App Engine, and you must pick or tune its environment.
An existing app has spiky traffic and must scale to zero at very low cost, which fits the standard environment.
An existing app needs a custom runtime or native code with steady traffic, which fits the flexible environment.
traps: App Engine for a new application is a wrong answer, because Google recommends Cloud Run.
The flexible environment does not scale to zero, because it keeps at least one instance.

confused.tell: For a new app or a modernization, Google recommends Cloud Run instead of App Engine.

services.name: Cloud Storage
services.what: Cloud Storage is object storage with no capacity limit. You choose a storage class from access frequency and a location type from availability needs.
cues: Uploaded files must survive when the autoscaler deletes the VMs that received them.
Access patterns vary by object, and nobody can predict which items stay popular.
Data must stay readable through a region outage under the same bucket name.
A large training dataset needs scalable, cost-efficient storage.
traps: A lifecycle rule moves objects only to colder classes, so only Autoclass moves read objects back to Standard.
Turbo replication works only for dual-region buckets, not for multi-region buckets.

confused.tell: Keep training datasets in Cloud Storage, and use Managed Lustre for synchronous checkpoints that need low latency.
Object Versioning does not stop a project owner from deleting backups, but a locked backup vault does.

services.name: Persistent Disk, Hyperdisk, and Local SSD
services.what: Persistent Disk, Hyperdisk, and Local SSD are the block storage options for Compute Engine VMs. Google recommends Hyperdisk, where you set performance separately from size.
cues: A database disk needs set IOPS and throughput, independent of its capacity.
A new N4 or C4 VM needs a durable data disk.
A disk needs an RPO of zero for a zone outage.
The workload needs the fastest scratch space or a cache, such as SQL Server tempdb.
traps: Local SSD data is lost on stop, suspend, or preemption by default, and snapshots cannot back it up.
Persistent Disk is not available on N4 or C4 VMs, and its performance grows only with disk size.

confused.tell: An NFS server on one VM with a regional disk is self-managed, so shared files go to Filestore.
Regional disks and Asynchronous Replication copy corruption and deletions, so recovery from them needs snapshots or backups.

services.aws: Amazon EBS (Local SSD maps to EC2 instance store)

services.name: Filestore
services.what: Filestore is managed NFS file storage. Use the Regional tier for resilience to a zone outage.
cues: Several VMs must read and write the same files over NFSv4.1 with POSIX file locking.
The shared file system must stay available if one zone fails.
GKE needs many small shares through the Filestore CSI driver.
traps: A Zonal tier instance becomes unavailable when its zone fails, so choose Regional for zone resilience.
Basic HDD and Basic SSD are legacy tiers, so do not pick them for a new resilient share.

confused.tell: Filestore serves NFS, so Windows SMB shares go to NetApp Volumes.
Cloud Storage FUSE is not POSIX compliant and is not NFS, so it cannot give file locking.
Thousands of HPC clients that write the same files in parallel need Managed Lustre, not an NFS share.

services.name: Google Cloud NetApp Volumes
services.what: Google Cloud NetApp Volumes is a managed file service. It supports NFS, SMB, iSCSI, and NVMe/TCP.
cues: Windows servers need SMB file shares on Google Cloud.
An NFS workload needs high performance, and zonal availability is enough.
traps: Only the Flex service levels offer regional pools.
You cannot create new Flex File pools from September 15, 2026.

confused.tell: Filestore serves NFS only, while NetApp Volumes also serves SMB.
NetApp Volumes is an NFS and SMB file service, not the parallel file system for HPC scratch data.

services.name: Managed Lustre
services.what: Managed Lustre is a managed parallel file system for AI, ML, and HPC, with up to 10 TBps of throughput. An instance is zonal.
cues: Thousands of VMs in one zone read and write the same scratch files in parallel, with POSIX semantics.
A large training job writes synchronous checkpoints often and needs low-latency file access from many Pods.
Model weights must load with low latency as an inference deployment scales out.
An HPC simulation moves from an on-premises Lustre cluster.
traps: Cluster Toolkit deprecated its Parallelstore blueprints, so choose Managed Lustre for new designs.
An instance is zonal, so deploy an instance in each zone for more availability.

confused.tell: Filestore is managed NFS, while the storage guidance names Managed Lustre for a parallel file system.
Cloud Storage holds datasets and asynchronous checkpoints, while Managed Lustre takes synchronous checkpoints.

services.name: Cloud Storage FUSE
services.what: Cloud Storage FUSE mounts a Cloud Storage bucket as a file system. Code can then read objects through a file path.
cues: Training code reads files from a file system path, and the data must stay in Cloud Storage.
Training nodes stream large sharded files, such as TFRecord, from a bucket.
A GKE inference deployment with limited node scaling loads model weights from a bucket.
traps: Do not use Cloud Storage FUSE as a POSIX file system or as a database disk.

confused.tell: FUSE is not POSIX compliant or NFS, so shared files with locking need Filestore.
Parallel POSIX reads and writes from many clients need Managed Lustre, not a FUSE mount.
FUSE gives the file path, while Rapid Cache adds a zonal read cache for repeated reads.

services.name: Rapid Cache
services.what: Rapid Cache is an SSD-backed zonal read cache for Cloud Storage. It fits data that changes rarely and is read often, such as model training data.
cues: Nodes in one zone reread a large, rarely changing dataset from a multi-region bucket every epoch.
The team wants higher read throughput and lower multi-region data transfer fees, and the data must stay in Cloud Storage.
A multi-region workload has strict performance needs.
traps: Rapid Cache is a read cache, so it does not help scratch data that needs parallel writes.

confused.tell: Rapid Cache does not change bucket replication, so a 15-minute RPO needs turbo replication on a dual-region.
Copying the dataset to Filestore moves it out of Cloud Storage, while Rapid Cache keeps it in the bucket.
Rapid Cache only caches reads, so parallel POSIX writes need Managed Lustre.

services.name: Backup and DR Service
services.what: Backup and DR Service gives central, policy-based backups for Compute Engine, Filestore, Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, and more. Its backup vaults keep backups immutable and indelible until the enforced retention ends.
cues: An attacker with stolen project owner credentials must not be able to delete VM or database backups.
Backups must stay recoverable after ransomware or accidental deletion.
A central team must manage backup policies for many service projects.
traps: Restore-based recovery is too slow for an RTO of minutes, so use a cross-region replica and a standby cluster.

confused.tell: A project owner can delete object versions, but no one can decrease a locked vault retention.
Snapshot schedules guarded only by IAM are not indelible, because an owner can grant the delete permission again.
A project owner can turn off Cloud SQL deletion protection, so it does not make backups indelible.

services.name: Cloud SQL
services.what: Cloud SQL is managed MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server for general-purpose relational workloads in one region. It scales vertically and uses read replicas for more reads.
cues: Self-managed MySQL or PostgreSQL on VMs takes too much patching and backup work.
MySQL or SQL Server databases must move to a managed service with small code changes.
The database must keep running through a zone failure.
Customer-facing apps must recover from a region outage in minutes.
traps: Cloud SQL HA uses two zones in one region, so it does not survive a region outage.
A read replica cannot fail over, and the HA standby cannot serve reads.

confused.tell: Cloud SQL writes go to one primary in one region, so global strongly consistent writes need Spanner.
The Cloud SQL data cache speeds up reads, but analytics on live data needs the AlloyDB columnar engine.
Bigtable is the documented fit for high-throughput time-series writes, not one relational instance.

services.aws: Amazon RDS (Cloud SQL HA maps to RDS Multi-AZ)

services.name: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
services.what: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL is a PostgreSQL-compatible managed database for demanding OLTP. Its columnar engine runs analytical queries on live transactional data (HTAP).
cues: Dashboard queries on live order data slow down transactions, and a nightly export makes them a day old.
A PostgreSQL app needs more performance, with no rewrite and no separate data pipeline.
HA failover must lose no data, and read pools must scale reads.
traps: Secondary clusters in other regions replicate asynchronously, so AlloyDB does not give Spanner-style global writes.

confused.tell: Cloud SQL runs analytical queries in the row store, where they compete with transactions.
A move to Spanner needs schema and application changes, while AlloyDB keeps PostgreSQL compatibility.
Datastream to BigQuery adds a pipeline and a second system, while AlloyDB runs analytics in the database.

services.name: Spanner
services.what: Spanner is a relational database that scales horizontally and gives external consistency by default. Multi-region configurations have a 99.999% SLA and need Enterprise Plus edition.
cues: A ledger for users on several continents needs SQL, ACID transactions, and the latest balance from any region.
The database must survive a full region failure and add write capacity without sharding.
Load peaks each evening, and capacity must follow it with no manual work.
traps: Multi-region Spanner for a regional app that accepts region downtime costs far more than needed.
Standard edition is regional only, so a multi-region design needs Enterprise Plus.

confused.tell: Cloud SQL cross-region replicas are asynchronous and read-only, while Spanner commits writes across regions.
Bigtable has no relational schema or multi-row ACID transactions, and Spanner has both.
An existing PostgreSQL app that must not change fits AlloyDB, because Spanner needs schema work.

services.aws: Amazon Aurora or Amazon DynamoDB (partial match)

services.name: Bigtable
services.what: Bigtable is a key-value NoSQL database for large amounts of single-keyed data. It gives low latency and high throughput for data such as time series and IoT readings.
cues: Vehicles send bursts of telemetry, and the app needs low-latency reads of recent readings per vehicle.
An Apache HBase application must move to a managed service with minimal code changes.
The workload needs over a million single-row reads and writes per second at millisecond latency.
traps: A row key that starts with a timestamp creates hotspots, so put a high-cardinality value first.
Multi-cluster routing is eventually consistent and has no single-row transactions, which need single-cluster routing.

confused.tell: BigQuery serves interactive SQL analytics, while Bigtable serves key-based reads and writes at high throughput.
A relational schema with multi-row ACID transactions needs Spanner, because Bigtable has neither.
Bigtable targets high-throughput server workloads, while Firestore has mobile clients with offline sync.

services.name: Firestore
services.what: Firestore is a serverless document NoSQL database with ACID transactions. It also offers a MongoDB-compatible API.
cues: Field workers must read and edit data offline and sync the changes when the network returns.
Other users' screens must update in real time when a record changes.
The team wants a document database with no capacity planning.
MongoDB applications must move to a managed service and keep their code and drivers.
traps: You cannot change the location or the data access mode of a Firestore database after you create it.
Use Datastore compatibility only for applications that depend on the Datastore APIs.

confused.tell: A relational ledger with SQL needs Spanner, because Firestore is a NoSQL document database.
Firestore client libraries give offline sync and real-time listeners, which Bigtable does not offer.
Memorystore is an in-memory store that you size, with no mobile offline sync or real-time listeners.

services.name: Memorystore
services.what: Memorystore is a managed in-memory key-value service for Valkey, Redis Cluster, and Redis. It fits caches and session data that need sub-millisecond access.
cues: Users lose shopping carts when the autoscaler deletes VMs that keep sessions in local memory.
A self-managed Redis server on a VM takes too much patching and replication work.
Redis data in a data center must move to a managed service with no engine change.
traps: Replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose acknowledged writes.
Memorystore for Memcached is deprecated, so choose Memorystore for Valkey for new caches.

confused.tell: Session affinity on the load balancer is best effort, so move session state to Memorystore instead.
Durable app data with offline sync belongs in Firestore, not in an in-memory store.

services.name: BigQuery
services.what: BigQuery is the serverless data warehouse for SQL analytics (OLAP) on Google Cloud. Compute and storage scale separately, so there is no cluster to size.
cues: Analysts run interactive SQL analytics or warehouse reports on large datasets.
A Teradata, Redshift, or Snowflake data warehouse moves to Google Cloud.
Data sits in Amazon S3 or Azure Blob Storage, must stay there, and only filtered results may move.
Analysts want ML or AI results on warehouse data, or on media in Cloud Storage, without moving the data.
traps: A multi-region dataset location gives no cross-region redundancy, so it is not a regional DR design.
Slot commitments exist only for the Enterprise and Enterprise Plus editions, not for Standard edition.

confused.tell: Cloud SQL serves transactional application reads and writes, while BigQuery is an analytics warehouse, not an OLTP or cache database.
Bigtable serves high-throughput, low-latency single-key reads and writes, while BigQuery serves interactive SQL analytics.
For analytics on live PostgreSQL data with no pipeline, the AlloyDB columnar engine fits better than a BigQuery copy.

services.name: Pub/Sub
services.what: Pub/Sub is an asynchronous messaging service that decouples the services that produce messages from the services that process them. Many subscriptions can receive each message, with at-least-once delivery by default.
cues: One event must reach several independent consumers, and one failed consumer must not stop the producer.
A slow backend, such as an old ERP, must receive orders at a rate it can handle.
Events from many clients or devices arrive in bursts and must be ingested and absorbed.
Messages already match a BigQuery table and must land there with no subscriber code.
traps: Exactly-once delivery works only on pull subscriptions in the same region, never on push or export subscriptions.
Delivery is at least once, so consumers must be idempotent to avoid double processing.

confused.tell: In Cloud Tasks the sender names one endpoint and controls rate and retries. Pub/Sub fans out with no publisher control.
Managed Kafka fits only when existing applications must keep Kafka, and Google recommends Pub/Sub for new streaming workloads.
Eventarc routes Google Cloud events, such as Cloud Storage changes, to targets, and it uses Pub/Sub as its transport.

services.name: Dataflow
services.what: Dataflow is a managed service that runs Apache Beam pipelines for batch and streaming data. It gives exactly-once processing by default.
cues: A stream needs counts or aggregates in event-time windows, and late events must be included.
The team builds a new batch or streaming pipeline with enrichment, custom sources, or a dead-letter table.
A streaming pipeline must scale automatically with no clusters for the team to manage.
traps: A Dataflow template that copies Pub/Sub messages into BigQuery unchanged adds a job to run and pay for.
When the stem rules out custom ETL code, a hand-written Dataflow pipeline is wrong even though it works.

confused.tell: If messages need no transformation, a Pub/Sub BigQuery subscription replaces the Dataflow job with less overhead.
Existing Spark jobs move to Managed Service for Apache Spark, because a Beam rewrite breaks a same-code requirement.
Managed Airflow orchestrates batch steps, while Dataflow processes the stream itself, including late data.

services.aws: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink

services.name: Managed Service for Apache Kafka
services.what: Managed Service for Apache Kafka runs managed Kafka clusters for existing Kafka workloads. You manage the cluster size and topic partitions, and you pay for provisioned vCPU, RAM, and local storage.
cues: Existing applications use Kafka and must keep using it.
A Pub/Sub Lite workload must move before its turndown on January 31, 2027.
traps: Managed Kafka for applications with no Kafka dependency adds cluster sizing and partition work that Pub/Sub avoids.

confused.tell: For new workloads, minimal configuration, or data movement between regions, Google recommends Pub/Sub.

docs.title: Managed Service for Apache Kafka overview

services.name: Managed Service for Apache Spark
services.what: Managed Service for Apache Spark runs Spark and Hadoop workloads in cluster or serverless deployments. The cluster deployment bills for uptime, and the serverless deployment bills for job runtime.
cues: A company shuts down a Hadoop cluster and wants to run the same Spark code on Google Cloud.
Intermittent Spark batch jobs must run with no clusters to manage, paid only while the jobs run.
The workload needs Hive, Flink, Trino, or Kafka on the cluster, or maximum control.
traps: Autoscaling an idle cluster down to save money is wrong. Delete idle clusters and use ephemeral clusters.
A cluster deployment with autoscaling still bills for uptime, so it misses a pay-only-while-jobs-run requirement.

confused.tell: Dataflow suits new Apache Beam pipelines, while Managed Spark runs existing Spark code without a rewrite.
Data Fusion builds visual, code-free pipelines on ephemeral Spark clusters, while Managed Spark runs your own Spark code.

docs.title: Compare Managed Service for Apache Spark serverless and cluster deployments

services.name: Managed Service for Apache Airflow
services.what: Managed Service for Apache Airflow is managed Apache Airflow for batch ETL and ELT workflows written as Python DAGs. It supports backfills and DAG re-runs, with seconds of latency between tasks.
cues: A team runs Airflow on its own VMs and wants to keep its DAGs but stop managing upgrades and scaling.
One flow spans an on-premises database, Spark jobs, a partner API, and model training on Agent Platform.
Batch data pipelines need dependencies, schedules, and backfills across BigQuery, Dataflow, and Spark.
traps: SQL-only transformations in BigQuery do not need an Airflow environment. Dataform or BigQuery pipelines can schedule them.
CPU-heavy or memory-heavy tasks do not belong on the Airflow nodes. Use KubernetesPodOperator or GKEStartPodOperator.

confused.tell: Workflows chains HTTP services with millisecond latency and waits on callbacks, while Airflow waits only by polling.
Agent Platform Pipelines fits container-based ML workflows that stay inside Agent Platform, while Airflow fits flows across many systems.
Application Integration connects business systems through connectors with little code, while Airflow needs Python DAGs and polls.

docs.title: Managed Service for Apache Airflow documentation

services.name: Datastream
services.what: Datastream is a serverless change data capture (CDC) service. It replicates changes from operational databases into BigQuery, Cloud Storage, or Apache Iceberg tables.
cues: Analysts need operational tables in BigQuery with minutes of delay, and the source database stays the system of record.
MySQL, SQL Server, or Oracle silos must feed one analytics store in near real time.
Replication must reach a private on-premises source with no servers for the team to manage.
traps: Datastream does not list Teradata as a source. Warehouse migrations use BigQuery Migration Service.
Delivery is at least once, so use the event metadata to remove duplicates in the destination.

confused.tell: Database Migration Service moves a database to a new primary in Cloud SQL or AlloyDB. Datastream keeps an analytics copy.
BigQuery Data Transfer Service loads on a schedule, so it cannot give minutes of delay from a changing database.
If dashboards must query live data with no separate pipeline, the AlloyDB columnar engine replaces the replication.

services.name: Cloud Data Fusion
services.what: Cloud Data Fusion is a code-free, visual service for ETL and ELT pipelines with prebuilt connectors. At run time, it runs each pipeline on an ephemeral Managed Service for Apache Spark cluster.
cues: Teams want to build ETL or ELT pipelines visually, with prebuilt connectors and no code.
The need is a data pipeline, not service orchestration or business-system integration.
traps: Developer and Basic are not the production editions. Enterprise is the edition for production.

confused.tell: Analysts who already write SQL in BigQuery fit Dataform, while Data Fusion would rebuild their logic in another tool.
Application Integration maps data between business systems such as Salesforce, while Data Fusion builds ETL and ELT pipelines.
A plain copy of messages into BigQuery fits a Pub/Sub BigQuery subscription, not a Data Fusion pipeline.

services.name: Knowledge Catalog
services.what: Knowledge Catalog is the Google Cloud catalog for data discovery, data lineage, data quality scans, and business glossaries. It works across stores such as BigQuery and Cloud Storage.
cues: Data is siloed across many BigQuery datasets and Cloud Storage buckets, and analysts cannot find trusted data.
Analysts must see where data came from, with lineage across pipelines.
The company needs a data management platform before it shares or monetizes its data.
traps: Cloud Asset Inventory searches resource metadata for audits, but it does not check data quality or trace lineage.
Data Catalog began a phased shutdown on June 1, 2026, so it does not belong in a new design.

confused.tell: Copying all datasets into one central BigQuery project adds copies and cost but gives no quality checks or lineage.
Sensitive Data Protection pseudonymizes identifiers such as driver IDs, while Knowledge Catalog gives discovery, quality, and lineage.

services.name: Eventarc
services.what: Eventarc routes events, such as Cloud Storage changes or audit log entries, to Cloud Run, Cloud Run functions, or Workflows. Eventarc Advanced adds a central bus, many-to-many routing, and event transformation.
cues: A file upload to a Cloud Storage bucket must start processing right away, with no polling.
New rows in a BigQuery table arrive at irregular times and must start a pipeline run soon after.
Many teams and projects must share one event bus, with filters on any attribute and event transformation.
traps: Eventarc Advanced does not meet the compliance standards that Eventarc Standard supports, so avoid it for regulated workloads.
An Eventarc Advanced bus is still choreography, so it gives no single view of a process or a managed wait.

confused.tell: Eventarc supports choreography, while Workflows orchestrates the whole process with one status view. An event can start a workflow.
For rate-limited calls to one endpoint, Cloud Tasks controls dispatch, while Eventarc Advanced routes events among many parties.
Cloud Scheduler runs jobs at fixed times, while Eventarc reacts to each event as it happens.

services.name: Workflows
services.what: Workflows is a serverless orchestrator that chains HTTP-based services, with definitions in YAML or JSON. It bills per step, holds state, and can wait for up to a year.
cues: A business process inside one team's bounded context needs one place to track the status of each item.
A step must wait days or weeks for a human approval, and the design must not poll.
Microservices or HTTP APIs must be chained with millisecond latency between steps.
traps: Moving Airflow DAGs to Workflows means a rewrite of every DAG in YAML or JSON.
Pure choreography for a process that the business must track end to end leaves no central place to troubleshoot.

confused.tell: Managed Airflow fits batch ETL written as Python DAGs, with seconds of latency and waits by polling.
Application Integration maps data between business systems with little code, while Workflows fits developers who orchestrate services.
Eventarc and Pub/Sub are choreography with no central view, while Workflows controls and records the whole flow.

services.name: Cloud Tasks
services.what: Cloud Tasks is a queue service with explicit invocation: the sender names one handler and controls delivery. It supports rate limits, scheduled delivery, retries, and deduplication of task creation.
cues: Calls to a partner API must stay under the partner's fixed rate limit.
Traffic spikes must be absorbed while the caller adds a task and returns at once.
Failed calls to one endpoint must be retried, with a limit on the number of attempts.
traps: Cloud Tasks guarantees delivery but not its timing, so it does not fit when a user waits for the result.
One Cloud Tasks queue cannot deliver each task to several services. Fan-out is a Pub/Sub feature.

confused.tell: Pub/Sub fans one message out to many subscribers, while Cloud Tasks has one handler for each task.
Eventarc Advanced filters, transforms, and routes events among many parties, and it is not a rate-control queue for one endpoint.

services.name: Cloud Scheduler
services.what: Cloud Scheduler runs jobs at fixed times. A job can start a workflow or publish a Pub/Sub message.
cues: Work must run on a fixed timetable, such as a nightly or monthly job.
A scheduled Pub/Sub message must start a pipeline run or another automated task.
traps: A fixed schedule does not follow real demand, so it cannot replace autoscaling on a Pub/Sub backlog.
A scheduled call to a Cloud Run service still hits the 60-minute request timeout. A three-hour run needs a Cloud Run job.

confused.tell: Work that reacts to an event, such as new data landing, needs Eventarc. A schedule runs even with no new data.
Scheduler jobs that call functions force you to rebuild the dependencies, retries, and schedules that Airflow DAGs already define.
Monthly OS patching with a disruption budget is a VM Manager patch deployment, not a Scheduler job with SSH scripts.

services.name: Application Integration
services.what: Application Integration is an Integration Platform as a Service (iPaaS) with a drag-and-drop editor and Integration Connectors. It connects, maps, and transforms data between business systems.
cues: Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Cloud SQL use different data structures and must exchange data.
Business analysts, not developers, build and maintain the flows with little or no code.
Supplier files arrive over SFTP, and the company wants a managed flow with built-in retries.
traps: The Connectors task has a 10 MB payload limit, so large batch ETL jobs belong in Dataflow.

confused.tell: Workflows orchestrates services for developers, so field mapping between business systems would still need custom code.
Managed Airflow runs Python DAGs for batch pipelines, while Application Integration suits real-time business transactions.
For ETL and ELT pipelines, Google recommends Cloud Data Fusion, while Application Integration targets business-system integration.

services.name: Apigee
services.what: Apigee is Google's full API management platform. Its proxy layer adds security, rate limiting, and mediation through policies, with API products, a developer portal, and monetization.
cues: Partners must register apps, get API keys, and read documentation without help from the company.
The business wants to charge API consumers by usage tier.
New applications must keep working without code changes when a legacy backend is replaced later.
All API traffic must stay in the company's data centers, but Google should run the management plane.
traps: Apigee hybrid has no Pay-as-you-go pricing, so production hybrid needs a Subscription.
The Quota policy enforces business contracts, while SpikeArrest protects the backend from sudden bursts.

confused.tell: API Gateway fits project-level APIs for serverless backends and has no developer portal, API products, or monetization.
A load balancer with Cloud Armor protects traffic but gives no app registration, portal, product tiers, or usage charges.

services.name: API Gateway and Cloud Endpoints
services.what: API Gateway is a fully managed, pay-per-use gateway for project-level APIs with serverless backends. Cloud Endpoints is the option where you run the ESP or ESPv2 proxy yourself, most often for gRPC.
cues: A serverless project exposes APIs at the project level, and consumers need no developer portal.
The team wants a managed gateway with API keys, JWT validation, and quotas, billed per call.
The team wants to run the gateway proxy next to its own backend, often for gRPC services.
traps: The Cloud Endpoints Portal shut down on March 21, 2023, so it cannot serve as a developer portal.
API Gateway cannot proxy to Google APIs such as BigQuery. It sends an ID token, and they need an access token.

confused.tell: A developer portal, API products, monetization, or API traffic that must stay on-premises points to Apigee.

services.name: VPC networks, subnets, and routes
patterns: (?i)dynamic routing mode|global dynamic routing|regional dynamic routing
services.what: A VPC network and its routes and firewall rules are global resources; its subnets are regional. Use custom mode networks in production, and plan every IP range before you build.
cues: Hybrid links are in one region, and VMs in other regions get no routes to on-premises.
Test VMs must run with no route to production systems, for example in a separate project and VPC network.
A GKE cluster needs a large Pod range, and almost all RFC 1918 space is already allocated.
traps: Regional dynamic routing mode is the gcloud default, so learned routes apply only in the Cloud Router's region.
Class E space for Pods can cause problems with on-premises hardware; Google recommends 100.64.0.0/10.

confused.tell: Cloud Router runs the BGP sessions; the dynamic routing mode is a VPC network setting that decides where learned routes apply.
A VPC network in each team project leaves each team in control; Shared VPC keeps one network under a central team.

services.name: Shared VPC
services.what: Shared VPC lets service projects use subnets of a VPC network in a central host project. A central team keeps control of subnets, routes, and firewall rules.
cues: A central network team must control all subnets, routes, and firewall rules, while app teams work in their own projects.
Each app team may deploy only in the regions that the network team approves for it.
On-premises connectivity is set up once and must serve VMs in many projects.
traps: Network User on the whole host project lets a team use every subnet in every region; grant it on subnets.
In Shared VPC, GKE cannot create Pod and Service secondary ranges; a host project Network Admin creates them first.

confused.tell: Peered networks stay administratively separate, so each team keeps its own firewall rules; Shared VPC is one central network.
Shared VPC works only inside one organization; NCC VPC spokes can join networks from another organization.

services.name: VPC Network Peering
services.what: VPC Network Peering connects two VPC networks, also across organizations, with full VM bandwidth. It is not transitive, and subnet ranges cannot overlap.
cues: A few VPC networks need full bandwidth, and policy allows only peering between them.
Compute Engine VMs must reach a Standard VMware Engine network over internal IP addresses.
Network virtual appliances must sit in the path between a hub network and spoke networks.
traps: Peering A to B and B to C does not let A reach C; peer A to C directly or use NCC.
Spokes reach on-premises through a peered hub only if the hub exports and the spokes import custom routes.

confused.tell: Peering is not transitive and needs a connection for each pair; NCC VPC spokes are transitive through one hub.
Peering fails with overlapping ranges and exchanges whole subnets; PSC uses NAT and exposes only one service.

services.name: Private Service Connect
services.what: Private Service Connect (PSC) reaches one published service, or Google APIs, through an internal IP address in your VPC network. It uses NAT, so consumer and producer do not coordinate IP ranges.
cues: A partner in another organization offers one API, and its subnet overlaps one of your ranges.
Workloads must reach Google APIs through an internal address that the network team chooses.
API traffic from on-premises must be processed in one named region and stay private.
A model endpoint must accept private calls from the VPC network and on-premises, with traffic splits.
traps: Peered VPC networks cannot reach a PSC endpoint for Google APIs, so each spoke needs its own endpoint.
The all-apis bundle also allows APIs that VPC Service Controls does not support; the vpc-sc bundle blocks them.

confused.tell: Private services access peers with a producer network through a range you allocate; PSC reaches one service with no range to allocate.
Private Google Access uses Google-owned VIP ranges and cannot reach regional endpoints; a PSC endpoint uses an address you choose.
Peering gives reachability to a whole network and fails with overlapping ranges; PSC reaches only the published service.

services.name: Private services access
services.what: Private services access connects your VPC network to a producer network for Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Memorystore, or Filestore. It is a VPC Network Peering to a range that you allocate.
cues: Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, or Memorystore needs a private IP address for VMs in one VPC network.
On-premises apps time out when they connect to a Cloud SQL private IP address over Interconnect.
Memorystore for Redis must be reachable from a Shared VPC network or from on-premises over VPN.
traps: Peered VPC networks cannot use a private services access connection, because peering is not transitive.
On-premises access needs custom routes exported on the peering and the allocated range advertised by Cloud Router.

confused.tell: Private Google Access reaches Google APIs such as Cloud Storage; private services access reaches service instances in a producer network.
PSC reaches a service from many networks, projects, or organizations; private services access serves one consumer VPC network.

services.name: Private Google Access
services.what: Private Google Access is a per-subnet setting that lets VMs without external IP addresses reach Google APIs and services. It gives no internet access. On-premises hosts use its VIP ranges over hybrid links.
cues: VMs have no external IP addresses and must write to Cloud Storage, and internet access is forbidden.
On-premises servers must reach Google APIs privately over Cloud Interconnect or Cloud VPN.
The private path must block Google APIs that VPC Service Controls does not support.
traps: On-premises hosts need DNS for a VIP domain and a Cloud Router custom advertisement, not the subnet setting.
private.googleapis.com also allows APIs that VPC Service Controls does not support; restricted.googleapis.com blocks them.

confused.tell: Cloud NAT gives outbound internet access; Private Google Access reaches only Google APIs and services.
Private services access reaches instances such as Cloud SQL in a producer network, not Google APIs.
Choose a PSC endpoint for an address you pick or a regional API endpoint; Private Google Access supports neither.

services.name: Direct VPC egress and Serverless VPC Access
services.what: Direct VPC egress sends traffic from Cloud Run into a VPC network without a connector. A Serverless VPC Access connector does the same through VMs that you pay for. Google recommends Direct VPC egress.
cues: A Cloud Run service must reach a private Memorystore instance at the lowest cost, with no extra VMs to manage.
A Cloud Run service must call a partner API from one static outbound IP address.
traps: With private-ranges-only egress, internet calls still leave from a dynamic IP pool; set all-traffic to use Cloud NAT.
A connector adds VMs that you pay for, and connectors do not scale in after a peak.

confused.tell: Direct VPC egress gives the path into the VPC network; Cloud NAT in that network gives the static outbound address.
Cloud Run ingress settings control who can reach the service; they give it no path into a VPC network.
Cloud Build reaches private networks through private pools, not through Serverless VPC Access.

services.aws: Lambda function attached to a VPC

docs.title: Compare Direct VPC egress and VPC connectors

services.name: Cloud NAT
services.what: Cloud NAT is software-defined address translation for outbound traffic from VMs without external IP addresses. Public NAT reaches the internet, and Private NAT reaches private networks, also with overlapping ranges.
cues: VMs without external IP addresses must call an internet API from source addresses that a partner allowlists.
Private VMs or GKE nodes need outbound internet access for updates and third-party APIs.
Two NCC spoke networks have overlapping subnet ranges and must communicate privately.
traps: Cloud NAT allows no unsolicited inbound connections, so it gives administrators or on-premises hosts no path to VMs.
Automatic NAT IP allocation adds and removes addresses, which breaks an allowlist; use manual assignment.

confused.tell: Private Google Access reaches Google APIs with no internet access; Public NAT opens outbound internet access.
Cloud NAT does no filtering of its own; Secure Web Proxy adds identity and URL rules for outbound HTTP(S).

services.name: Application Load Balancer
services.what: The Application Load Balancer is a Layer 7 proxy for HTTP(S). The global external mode gives one anycast IP address for backends in many regions, with Cloud CDN and Cloud Armor.
cues: Users in many countries need lower latency and one public IP address for a web app.
An internal HTTPS API must survive a region failure and must not be reachable from the internet.
The same Cloud Run service runs in two regions and needs one global IP, caching, and WAF rules.
A one-country site needs the lowest network cost and Cloud Armor WAF rules.
traps: Only external load balancers are global; internal multi-region designs need the cross-region internal Application Load Balancer.
Serverless NEGs do not support health checks; use outlier detection to move requests away from a bad region.

confused.tell: Application Load Balancers carry only HTTP(S); UDP or an unchanged client IP needs a passthrough Network Load Balancer.
Cloud DNS routing policies switch users between regional load balancers; they do not give one global IP address.
A load balancer with Cloud Armor protects traffic but gives no developer portal, API products, or monetization.

services.aws: Application Load Balancer (one per region in AWS)

services.name: Network Load Balancers (proxy and passthrough)
services.what: Network Load Balancers work at Layer 4. Proxy modes carry TCP and end the client connection. Passthrough modes deliver packets unchanged and carry TCP, UDP, and other IP protocols.
cues: Game servers receive UDP from the internet and read the client source IP address in each packet.
Non-HTTP TCP traffic needs a load balancer, with optional SSL offload.
Appliance VMs must be the next hop of a static route.
traps: Proxy Network Load Balancers do not carry UDP and do not keep the client IP address in the packet.
Passthrough Network Load Balancers do not support serverless NEGs, so they cannot front Cloud Run.

confused.tell: A proxy Network Load Balancer can carry HTTPS, but Google says to use an Application Load Balancer for it.

services.name: Cloud CDN and Media CDN
services.what: Cloud CDN caches content at Google's edge for the global external and classic Application Load Balancers. You enable it on a backend service or backend bucket. Media CDN complements it for streaming video and large downloads.
cues: Static assets for users worldwide must load faster and put less load on the origin.
Media files in a Cloud Storage bucket are served to many users through a backend bucket.
The workload is streaming video or large file downloads.
traps: Cloud CDN caches responses, so it is wrong for patient data or other user-specific content.
Cloud CDN does not work with regional external Application Load Balancers or with Standard Tier.

confused.tell: Cloud CDN caches HTTP responses at the edge; Memorystore caches sessions and query results inside your VPC network.
Cloud CDN caches responses; it does not change the storage class of objects in the bucket.

services.name: Cloud DNS
services.what: Cloud DNS hosts your Google Cloud zones and resolves names across VPC networks and hybrid links. Its routing policies with health checks can also send users to another region.
cues: VMs must resolve an on-premises zone, and on-premises servers must resolve a Cloud DNS private zone.
A configuration error in the global load balancer must not take the site down.
Several VPC networks must resolve on-premises names through one network that forwards to on-premises.
traps: Cloud DNS does not support zone transfers.
Forwarded queries come from 35.199.192.0/19, so Cloud Router must advertise that range to on-premises.

confused.tell: VPC Network Peering does not change name resolution; Cloud DNS peering zones share zones between networks.
A global load balancer fails over behind one IP; DNS failover depends on resolvers that cache answers for the TTL.

services.name: Cloud Interconnect
services.what: Cloud Interconnect gives private, high-throughput links from your network to VPC networks through Dedicated Interconnect or Partner Interconnect. Traffic stays off the public internet, but it is not encrypted by default.
cues: Hybrid ingestion needs tens of Gbps, no public internet, and encryption between your router and Google's edge.
The hybrid link is mission-critical and must qualify for the 99.99% SLA.
Your routers cannot meet Google in a colocation facility, or you need less than a full 10-Gbps connection.
