Policy requires IPsec for all hybrid traffic, and the traffic must stay on the private link.
traps: Two connections in one metro give only 99.9%; the multi-region 99.99% topology needs four connections in two metros.
You cannot add IPsec to an existing VLAN attachment; you select encryption when you create it.

confused.tell: HA VPN over the internet encrypts traffic but crosses the internet; Google positions it for lower bandwidth needs.
Dedicated and Partner Interconnect connect on-premises networks; Cross-Cloud Interconnect connects to another cloud provider.

services.name: Cross-Cloud Interconnect
services.what: Cross-Cloud Interconnect gives dedicated physical connections between Google Cloud and AWS, Microsoft Azure, OCI, or Alibaba Cloud. It supports MACsec.
cues: Apps on another major cloud exchange large volumes of data with Google Cloud, and traffic must avoid the internet.
The team wants dedicated capacity to another cloud without managing cross-connects and routers.
traps: Direct Peering is not the answer for another cloud; Google recommends Cross-Cloud Interconnect.

confused.tell: Dedicated Interconnect connects on-premises networks; sending cloud-to-cloud traffic through a data center adds hops.
NCC site-to-site data transfer links your plants and offices; Cross-Cloud Interconnect is for other cloud providers.

services.name: Cloud VPN (HA VPN)
services.what: Cloud VPN connects your network, or another VPC network, to a VPC network through IPsec tunnels. HA VPN has two interfaces, uses only BGP, and gives 99.99% with a tunnel on each interface.
cues: The hybrid link needs lower cost or lower bandwidth, or it is for migration tests.
The on-premises VPN device has one public IP address, and the design needs the 99.99% SLA.
Policy requires IPsec on Cloud Interconnect traffic.
Two VPC networks in different projects or organizations need an encrypted link.
traps: Classic VPN has one interface and a 99.9% SLA, and you cannot create new Classic VPN tunnels that use BGP.
An HA VPN gateway with a tunnel on only one interface has no SLA.

confused.tell: Choose Cloud Interconnect for high throughput off the internet; HA VPN over the internet fits lower bandwidth.
HA VPN to a transit network is transitive but needs gateways and tunnels per network; NCC manages spokes from one hub.

services.name: Cloud Router
services.what: Cloud Router is the managed service that runs the BGP sessions for HA VPN tunnels, VLAN attachments, and Router appliance. The VPC dynamic routing mode decides if its routes cover one region or all regions.
cues: On-premises must learn a range that is not a local subnet, such as an API VIP range.
On-premises apps cannot reach a Cloud SQL private IP address that uses private services access.
VMs in other regions cannot use hybrid links that terminate in one region.
traps: Default advertisement sends only this network's subnets; API VIPs, 35.199.192.0/19, and peered ranges need custom advertisements.
You cannot change a Cloud Router's ASN later, and Partner Interconnect needs ASN 16550.

confused.tell: The dynamic routing mode is set on the VPC network; a new Cloud Router in another region cannot use existing attachments.
NCC connects many networks and sites through one hub; Cloud Router runs the BGP sessions on each link.

services.name: Network Connectivity Center
services.what: Network Connectivity Center (NCC) is a global hub. Its spokes hold VPC networks, HA VPN tunnels, VLAN attachments, or Router appliance VMs. VPC spokes give transitive connectivity, and the hub is control plane only.
cues: Many VPC networks, some in another organization, must reach each other with one point of management.
Plants and headquarters must exchange traffic over Google's network without a link for each pair of sites.
Two networks with overlapping ranges need private connectivity now, and the services have no load balancers.
traps: Site-to-site data transfer is best effort and works only in supported locations.
VPC spokes do not exchange static routes, and you cannot change the hub topology after you create it.

confused.tell: Peering is not transitive and always exchanges subnet routes; VPC spokes are transitive and support export filters.
Shared VPC is one network inside one organization; NCC joins separate networks, also across organizations.
Cross-Cloud Interconnect links to another cloud provider; NCC site-to-site data transfer links your own sites.

services.name: Network Service Tiers
services.what: Network Service Tiers set how internet traffic reaches a resource. In Premium Tier, the default, traffic enters Google's network close to the user. In Standard Tier, which costs less, it enters near the resource's region.
cues: A regional, latency-tolerant endpoint, such as a nightly file export, must cost less.
Users are on several continents, and the site uses a global load balancer and Cloud CDN.
One project has a global website and a regional endpoint with different cost goals.
traps: You choose the tier per resource, so one project can use both tiers.
Standard Tier does not support global load balancers or Cloud CDN.

confused.tell: The global external Application Load Balancer needs Premium Tier; with Standard Tier, use a regional external one.
Cloud CDN always uses Premium Tier, so Standard Tier cannot lower the cost of a CDN-backed site.

services.name: Network Intelligence Center
services.what: Network Intelligence Center is a set of tools for network troubleshooting and monitoring. It includes Connectivity Tests, Performance Dashboard, Network Topology, Network Analyzer, Firewall Insights, and Flow Analyzer.
cues: After a firewall change, the team must find which rule or route drops traffic between two VMs.
The team must prove that a path works before and after a change, without waiting for real traffic.
The team must tell whether a problem is in the application or in the network.
traps: A could-be-delivered result from Connectivity Tests does not guarantee delivery on the data plane.
Connectivity Tests does not count the real connections that a rule blocks; firewall rules logging records them.

confused.tell: Flow logs record traffic that already happened; Connectivity Tests analyzes the configured path without real traffic.
Packet Mirroring copies traffic to a collector; it does not analyze firewall rules and routes.

services.name: Cloud Armor
services.what: Cloud Armor automatically protects global external and classic Application Load Balancers and external proxy Network Load Balancers from DDoS attacks. Security policies on backend services add WAF rules, rate limiting, and geography rules. Edge policies act before the Cloud CDN cache; backend policies see only cache misses.
cues: A public web app behind a load balancer must block SQL injection and cross-site scripting.
A client that sends too many login requests must be blocked for a set time.
Users in a blocked country can still load cached content.
traps: Cache hits never reach a backend security policy; put geography blocks for cached content in an edge policy.
Direct calls to a Cloud Run run.app URL bypass Cloud Armor; set ingress to Internal and Cloud Load Balancers.

confused.tell: Firewall rules apply at the VMs, not at the Google Front Ends; Cloud Armor filters requests at the load balancer.
Cloud Armor protects apps from web attacks and DDoS; it does not stop data copies out of BigQuery or Cloud Storage.
Model Armor screens LLM prompts and responses; Cloud Armor does not decide whether a model response is unsafe.

services.name: Cloud NGFW (firewall rules and policies)
services.what: Cloud NGFW is the distributed, stateful firewall for VMs and supported load balancers. Rules live in VPC firewall rules or in hierarchical, global, or regional firewall policies. The Enterprise tier blocks threats inline.
cues: App teams choose which VMs get each firewall role, but they must not change the rules.
Exploits and command-and-control traffic must be blocked between tiers, without appliances or route changes.
The organization needs firewall rules that no project can override.
An auditor needs evidence of the connections that one deny rule blocks.
traps: A policy deny at high priority still loses to an earlier VPC firewall rule allow, unless you set BEFORE_CLASSIC_FIREWALL.
Network tags are not a security boundary, because anyone who can edit a VM can change them.

confused.tell: A Cloud IDS endpoint covers its region but only alerts; Cloud NGFW Enterprise endpoints are zonal and block inline.
Cloud Armor protects traffic through load balancers; Cloud NGFW rules apply at each VM, also east-west.
FQDN objects and URL filtering cannot match a URL path; Secure Web Proxy can, with TLS inspection.

services.name: Cloud IDS and Packet Mirroring
services.what: Cloud IDS is a managed intrusion detection service that inspects a copy of traffic from Packet Mirroring. It detects threats and alerts, but it does not block them. Packet Mirroring copies full packets, payloads included.
cues: A compliance rule, such as PCI 11.4 or HIPAA, requires threat detection on network traffic.
The team needs full packet payloads for deep forensics or a third-party IDS.
traps: Cloud IDS cannot meet a requirement to block exploits.
Packet Mirroring uses VM bandwidth and does not record which firewall rule allowed or denied a connection.

confused.tell: Cloud NGFW Enterprise intrusion prevention blocks threats inline; Cloud IDS only alerts.
VPC Flow Logs hold only sampled connection records; Packet Mirroring captures full packets.
Connectivity Tests analyzes firewall rules and routes; Packet Mirroring only copies traffic.

services.aws: Traffic mirroring with a third-party IDS

services.name: Secure Web Proxy
services.what: Secure Web Proxy is a managed proxy for outbound HTTP and HTTPS. It denies all traffic by default, allows traffic by source identity and destination, and logs each request.
cues: Only VMs that run as one service account may call one partner host and URL path.
Compliance needs a log entry for each outbound HTTP request.
All other outbound web traffic must be denied from one central point.
traps: Matching a URL path in HTTPS traffic needs TLS inspection.
With Shared VPC, Secure Web Proxy runs only in the host project.

confused.tell: Cloud NAT gives internet egress with no filtering of its own; Secure Web Proxy adds identity and URL rules.
FQDN objects work at the network layer, and URL filtering sees only the domain and SNI; neither matches a URL path.
VPC Service Controls protects Google Cloud APIs; it does not control traffic to third-party hosts.

services.name: VPC Service Controls
services.what: VPC Service Controls puts a perimeter around projects and their Google-managed services, such as Cloud Storage and BigQuery. It blocks API requests that cross the perimeter, even with valid credentials. Use it with IAM.
cues: Stolen or valid credentials must not copy BigQuery or Cloud Storage data to a project outside the company.
Analysts may query the protected data only from the corporate network.
A new perimeter must go live without breaking legitimate data flows.
traps: A perimeter does not choose where a service stores data, and it does not add CMEK.
A perimeter does not block third-party APIs or services on the internet.

confused.tell: IAM decides who can act; a perimeter blocks data movement across its boundary even when IAM allows it.
Organization policies restrict configuration, such as resource locations; a perimeter controls API requests across its boundary.
Cloud Armor protects web apps behind load balancers; it does not control copies out of BigQuery or Cloud Storage.

services.name: IAM (roles, conditions, and deny policies)
services.what: IAM decides who can do what on which resource. Allow policies grant roles, and deny policies and principal access boundary policies take access away.
cues: A group must lose one inherited permission in one project, and all its other access must stay the same.
No predefined role gives least privilege, so the design needs a custom role.
Access must end at a set time, or apply only to resources with a certain tag.
A security review flags the Owner or Editor basic role on a workload or a group.
traps: A more restrictive allow binding on the project cannot remove an inherited grant, because allow policies are a union.
An IAM condition has no effect when the principal also holds the same role without a condition.

confused.tell: Removing a role changes who can act; an organization policy restricts what anyone can configure, including owners.
IAM grants access to principals; a perimeter blocks data copies out of it even with valid credentials.
A conditional binding fits one known time window; PAM fits on-demand elevation with justification and approval.

services.name: Resource hierarchy (organization, folders, projects)
services.what: The organization, folders, and projects that hold all Google Cloud resources. Allow, deny, and organization policies on a node are inherited by everything below it.
cues: A team needs the same access in every current and future project under one folder.
Business units or environments need separate administration and separate policies.
An untrusted workload must be isolated, so it needs its own project as a trust boundary.
Projects must belong to the company, not to the employee who created them.
traps: A grant on the organization also reaches projects outside the target folder, which breaks least privilege.
Moving a project to another folder changes every inherited policy, so it cannot fix one permission.

confused.tell: An ordinary folder groups projects and passes down policies; an Assured Workloads folder also applies a predefined control package.
A folder groups projects for access and policy; App Hub groups resources from several projects into one application.

services.name: Organization Policy Service
services.what: Organization Policy Service restricts how resources can be configured, for everyone, including project owners. A policy on an organization, folder, or project applies to its descendants.
cues: No VM in any project may have an external IP address, whatever roles people have.
Teams may create resources only in approved regions, with no manual review of each project.
CMEK must be mandatory, and keys may come only from approved key projects.
Project owners must not turn off a control such as OS Login, or Binary Authorization on Cloud Run.
traps: Most constraints are not retroactive, so existing resources that violate them keep running until you fix them.
Dry-run mode only logs violations; it does not enforce the policy or fix existing resources.

confused.tell: Removing a role changes who can act; a constraint changes what anyone can configure.
The resource locations constraint limits where new resources go; it has no support access controls.
Security Command Center finds a misconfiguration after it exists; an organization policy blocks it at create or update time.

services.name: Service accounts and impersonation
services.what: Service accounts are identities for workloads, not people. Impersonation lets a caller get short-lived credentials for a service account instead of using a key.
cues: A developer must test on a laptop with exactly the permissions of a service account, and key creation is blocked.
An engineer must run Terraform as a deployer service account, with least privilege.
A build, pipeline, or job runs as a shared default service account with the Editor role.
The team must control which users can run jobs as a pipeline's service account.
traps: Service Account User only lets you attach a service account; impersonation needs Service Account Token Creator.
Token Creator on the project lets the user impersonate every service account in that project.

confused.tell: A workload outside Google Cloud uses Workload Identity Federation; a Google identity impersonates with Token Creator.
Service accounts are for workloads; employees get user accounts through Cloud Identity.
A service account key in Secret Manager is still a long-lived key; impersonation or federation removes it.

docs.title: Best practices for using service accounts securely

services.name: Cloud Identity and Google Cloud Directory Sync
services.what: Cloud Identity is Google's identity as a service product for users and groups, without Workspace applications. Google Cloud Directory Sync (GCDS) provisions users and groups into it from Active Directory.
cues: Employees must sign in with their Active Directory credentials, and Active Directory MFA must still apply.
Deleting a user in Active Directory must also remove the user from Google Cloud.
The company needs an organization resource but does not use Google Workspace.
traps: GCDS does not sync passwords; SAML SSO sends authentication to Active Directory.
Managed Service for Microsoft AD serves workloads; it does not provision Cloud Identity users or configure SSO.

confused.tell: GCDS syncs accounts into Cloud Identity; Workforce Identity Federation gives SSO with no account sync.
Employees need user accounts; service accounts are identities for workloads.

services.name: Workload Identity Federation
services.what: Workload Identity Federation swaps an external workload's own credential, such as a GitHub OIDC token, for a short-lived Google token. Workload Identity Federation for GKE gives each Kubernetes ServiceAccount its own IAM identity.
cues: GitHub Actions, AWS, Azure, or on-premises workloads deploy to Google Cloud, and stored keys must go.
Only workflows from the company's own GitHub organization may deploy.
GKE Pods need access to one bucket with least privilege and no keys.
traps: GitHub uses one issuer for all organizations, so the provider needs an attribute condition on your organization's numeric ID.
All GKE clusters in one project share one workload identity pool, so put an untrusted cluster in another project.

confused.tell: Federate when code runs outside Google Cloud or in GKE Pods; attach a dedicated service account to other Google Cloud resources.
Cloud Identity and Workforce Identity Federation sign in people; Workload Identity Federation authenticates automated workloads.

services.name: Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)
services.what: IAP checks the user's identity and IAM role before a request reaches an HTTPS app, so users need no VPN. IAP TCP forwarding gives SSH and RDP to VMs with no external IP address.
cues: Only employees may reach an internal web app, and the team wants no VPN or servers to manage.
Admins need SSH to VMs with no external IP address, and the company wants no bastion host or VPN.
IAM must decide who can open an admin tunnel, with an optional device or network condition.
traps: IAP on a load balancer does not stop direct traffic to the backends; add firewall rules and verify the signed header.
For IAP TCP forwarding, allow ingress only from 35.235.240.0/20, not from 0.0.0.0/0.

confused.tell: A VPN checks the network path; IAP checks the user's identity and IAM role on each request or tunnel.
IAP decides who can open the tunnel; OS Login decides who can log in to the VM and who gets sudo.
IAP enforces access; device-based access levels and apps outside Google Cloud need Chrome Enterprise Premium.

services.aws: Application Load Balancer with Cognito, AWS Verified Access

services.name: Chrome Enterprise Premium
services.what: Chrome Enterprise Premium is Google's zero trust access product. It adds device and time-based access levels, access to non-Google Cloud apps, and threat and data loss protection in Chrome.
cues: Admins may connect only from company-managed laptops that run Endpoint Verification.
Web apps on-premises, on AWS, or on Azure need the same identity and context checks.
Access must depend on device security posture or time of day, not only on the IP address.
traps: A VPN or office IP allowlist checks the network, not the device, so any device on that network gets in.
Chrome Enterprise Core comes at no additional cost, but it has no device posture or time-based access levels.

confused.tell: IAP enforces access levels on apps and tunnels; device attributes in those levels need Chrome Enterprise Premium.
OS Login 2-step verification checks the user, not the device.

services.name: OS Login
services.what: OS Login controls SSH access to VMs with IAM roles instead of SSH keys in metadata. roles/compute.osLogin gives login without sudo, and roles/compute.osAdminLogin gives login with sudo.
cues: Engineers add their own SSH keys to project metadata, and IAM must decide who logs in.
A removed employee must lose VM access as soon as the role is removed.
Every SSH login needs a second factor, and project owners must not be able to turn OS Login off.
traps: For 2-step verification, set both enable-oslogin and enable-oslogin-2fa to TRUE.
Every user who logs in can use the permissions of the VM's service account, so keep that account minimal.

confused.tell: IAP TCP forwarding gives the network path to a VM with no external IP; OS Login decides who can log in.
A firewall rule controls the network path; it does not control which users log in or require a second factor.

services.name: Privileged Access Manager
services.what: Privileged Access Manager gives temporary, on-demand role grants. An entitlement sets who can request which roles, for how long, and whether a justification or approval is needed.
cues: Engineers need emergency or on-demand elevated access, with a justification and an approval.
Elevated roles must end automatically, and audit logs must record the access.
traps: You cannot add an expiry condition to the Owner role; use a predefined role with a condition, or PAM.

confused.tell: A conditional binding with an expiry fits one known time window; PAM fits repeated requests for elevation.
Impersonation lends a service account's permissions for a short task; approvals and justifications need PAM.

services.name: Cloud KMS (CMEK and Autokey)
services.what: Cloud KMS is Google's managed key service. As a customer-managed encryption key (CMEK), your key wraps the data keys of services such as BigQuery and Cloud Storage.
cues: The company must control rotation, disable keys, or log key use, which default encryption cannot do.
The security team manages keys but must not decrypt data, and app teams must not manage keys.
Developers must get CMEK on new resources without a manual key request process.
traps: The key must be in the same exact location as the resource, and key rings cannot move.
Rotation creates a new key version but does not re-encrypt existing data.

confused.tell: Cloud KMS never returns key material; store passwords and API keys in Secret Manager.
Choose HSM keys only when a requirement names hardware protection or FIPS 140-2 Level 3.
CMEK protects data at rest; data in memory needs Confidential Computing.

services.name: Cloud HSM
services.what: Cloud HSM keys are Cloud KMS keys with the HSM protection level. Google manages the FIPS 140-2 Level 3 HSMs, and the keys use the same Cloud KMS API.
cues: Policy says keys must be generated and stored in hardware validated to FIPS 140-2 Level 3.
The company must control rotation and disable keys, but will not operate HSM hardware.
A team needs cryptographic isolation and administrative control of dedicated HSM partitions (single-tenant Cloud HSM).
traps: Default encryption uses Level 1 validated modules, so it does not meet a Level 3 hardware requirement.
The protection level is fixed when you create a key, so a software key cannot become an HSM key.

confused.tell: Cloud HSM key material stays inside Google Cloud; choose Cloud EKM when keys must stay outside Google.
Software keys use Level 1 validated modules, so they do not meet a hardware requirement.

services.name: Cloud EKM
services.what: Cloud EKM keeps key material in a supported external key manager outside Google Cloud. Google does not store or cache the keys, so data is unavailable when the key manager is unavailable.
cues: A regulation says key material must never be inside Google.
The company or a partner runs the key manager and must be able to deny key use from outside.
Each key use needs a reason that the company can deny, with Key Access Justifications in Assured Workloads.
traps: The internet path to the key manager risks latency and availability problems; Google suggests Cloud EKM over a VPC network.
Key Access Justifications works only with Assured Workloads, not on keys in ordinary projects.

confused.tell: Cloud HSM keeps key material in Google-managed HSMs; only Cloud EKM keeps it outside Google.
Access Approval gates Google personnel access to data; a reason for every key use needs Key Access Justifications.

services.name: Secret Manager
services.what: Secret Manager stores secret values, such as passwords, API keys, and certificates, that a principal with access can read. It is the recommended way to give a build a secret.
cues: A build or service needs a partner API token that must never be in source control or build configuration.
Only one pipeline's identity may read a token, while other teams run builds in the same project.
Secret changes must be tested and rolled back with the release process.
traps: A rotation schedule only sends Pub/Sub messages; you write the code that adds the new version.
Reading the latest alias lets a bad new version break new instances; pin a version number instead.

confused.tell: Cloud KMS keeps keys that you cannot view or export; Secret Manager returns the secret value to authorized callers.
A service account key stored as a secret is still a long-lived key; federation removes the key.

services.name: Security Command Center
services.what: Security Command Center finds misconfigurations, vulnerabilities, and threats across projects. The Standard tier has no additional charge, and Premium adds threat detection, attack paths, and compliance monitoring.
cues: The security team wants threat detection and attack paths across the whole organization.
The team needs an inventory of AI assets and findings about threats to them.
Web apps need scans for cross-site scripting, outdated libraries, and mixed content.
traps: Threat detection needs the Premium tier, and Google lists the Enterprise tier as deprecated.
Detection after deployment lets a noncompliant resource exist, so it fails a block-before-create requirement.

confused.tell: Security Command Center reports a misconfiguration after it exists; an organization policy blocks it at create time.
Security Command Center detects threats; a VPC Service Controls perimeter reduces data exfiltration.
AI Protection reports AI risks; Model Armor floor settings stop developers from creating weak templates.

services.name: Sensitive Data Protection
services.what: Sensitive Data Protection discovers, inspects, and de-identifies sensitive data such as PII. It includes Cloud DLP and can redact, mask, or tokenize values.
cues: Customers type phone numbers or addresses, and those values must never reach stored history or logs.
Analysts must join records on identifiers without seeing the original values.
Downstream systems must use tokens instead of card numbers to narrow PCI DSS scope.
The company must find where PII lives across an organization, folder, or project.
traps: A nightly scan finds data after it is stored; values that must never be stored need redaction before the write.
Hashes and transient keys cannot be reversed; to re-identify later, use AES-SIV or FPE with a KMS-wrapped key.

confused.tell: Model Armor screens live prompts and responses; Sensitive Data Protection defines the data types and scans stored data.
CMEK encrypts stored data, but the sensitive values stay stored and readable by users with access.

services.name: Model Armor
services.what: Model Armor screens LLM prompts and responses for prompt injection, jailbreaks, sensitive data, harmful content, and malicious URLs. It works for models in Google Cloud and in other clouds.
cues: A chatbot must stop prompt injection, jailbreaks, and unsafe responses with one central policy outside the code.
Every template in a folder must include prompt injection detection, also in future projects.
No prompt may reach a model without a completed check, even during a Model Armor outage.
Users must see a masked card number in a model response instead of an error.
traps: "Inspect only" logs violations but blocks nothing; switch to "Inspect and block" after you tune the template.
The Agent Platform integration skips screening on a Model Armor error; call the API from the app to block unscreened prompts.

confused.tell: Cloud Armor filters web attacks at a load balancer; it does not judge whether a model response is unsafe.
A perimeter reduces exfiltration at the API boundary; it does not inspect prompt or response content.
Model Armor screens LLM app traffic; moderating a media library with a custom policy calls for Gemini.

services.name: Binary Authorization
services.what: Binary Authorization enforces a deploy-time policy on GKE and Cloud Run. Only images with the required attestations, such as a Cloud Build or QA sign-off, deploy.
cues: A QA lead must approve each image, and GKE must refuse images without that approval.
Only images that Cloud Build built may deploy to production.
An image that failed a vulnerability check must not deploy.
traps: On Cloud Run, developers can turn Binary Authorization off unless the run.allowedBinaryAuthorizationPolicies constraint requires it.
Cloud Run supports only the default rule; specific rules are for GKE.

confused.tell: Artifact Analysis reports vulnerabilities; Binary Authorization blocks a deploy that lacks the required attestation.
Cloud Armor filters HTTP requests; it does not control which images a cluster runs.
Binary Authorization governs container deploys; a virtual repository controls which package source wins.

services.name: Artifact Analysis
services.what: Artifact Analysis scans images pushed to Artifact Registry for vulnerabilities, and rechecks images pulled in the last 30 days. On-Demand Scanning can scan in a build and stop it.
cues: The team wants visibility of known vulnerabilities across all images in the registry.
Vulnerable images must be stopped in the build, before they reach the registry or production.
Auditors want proof that an image had no critical vulnerabilities when it was built.
traps: Enabling the Container Scanning API does not scan images already in the registry; push them again.
Scans are keyed to the image digest, so a new or changed tag does not start a new scan.

confused.tell: Automatic scanning only reports; Binary Authorization blocks the deploy, and On-Demand Scanning can fail the build.
Scanning does not make images or dependencies more available; remote and multi-region repositories do.

services.name: Confidential Computing
services.what: Confidential Computing protects data in use, in memory, with a hardware trusted execution environment. Confidential VM protects a whole VM, and Confidential Space lets parties process shared data that the operator cannot access.
cues: Data must stay encrypted in memory while the application processes it.
Several parties must compute on combined sensitive data that the workload operator cannot see.
An AI workload on GPUs or GKE nodes must protect data in use.
traps: A VPC Service Controls perimeter guards Google APIs; it does not protect VM memory.

confused.tell: CMEK controls keys for data at rest; it does not encrypt data in memory.
Shielded VM protects the boot chain against rootkits; Confidential VM protects data in memory.
Sole-tenant nodes isolate hardware for your project; they do not encrypt memory.

services.name: Assured Workloads
services.what: Assured Workloads applies a control package, such as EU Data Boundary or FedRAMP High, to a folder. Organization policy constraints and other features then enforce data location, personnel access, and key management controls.
cues: Data must stay in EU regions, and only EU-based support staff may access it, with predefined controls.
A regime such as FedRAMP High, IL5, ITAR, or CJIS applies to the workload.
Every key use needs a justification that the customer can deny.
traps: The EU Data Boundary package sets location controls only; EU-based support needs a package that adds support controls.
Residency commitments cover Customer Data at rest, not resource names or labels, so keep PHI out of metadata.

confused.tell: The resource locations constraint limits where new resources go; it has no support access controls.
CMEK controls keys, not where data is stored or who can support it.
Assured Workloads runs in the public cloud; Google Distributed Cloud air-gapped runs in your own data center.

services.name: Access Transparency and Access Approval
services.what: Access Transparency logs the actions of Google personnel on your Customer Data, with the reason and the accessor's location. Access Approval makes Google personnel get your administrator's approval first.
cues: A regulator requires that Google staff cannot access data until a named administrator approves each request.
Auditors want a record of what Google personnel did with Customer Data.
traps: Access Transparency logs record access after it happens; only Access Approval stops unapproved access.
Access Transparency is on by default at no extra charge, so it needs no support upgrade.

confused.tell: Cloud Audit Logs record your principals, including Google staff that you grant IAM roles; Access Transparency records other Google personnel access.
Access Approval gates access to data; a reason for every key use needs Key Access Justifications in Assured Workloads.
A perimeter controls API requests by context; it adds no approval step for Google personnel.

services.name: Cloud Audit Logs
services.what: Cloud Audit Logs records the actions of your own principals on Google Cloud. Admin Activity logs are always on, and Data Access logs are off by default for most services.
cues: An auditor asks who deleted a VM or changed a firewall rule or an IAM binding.
Auditors need a record of every object read, or of who called a prediction endpoint.
Audit logs from all current and future projects must be kept for years in one place.
traps: The _Required bucket keeps logs for a fixed 400 days, so longer retention needs a sink to another destination.
Data Access logs are off by default for most services, so object reads are not logged until you enable them.

confused.tell: Access Transparency records Google personnel; Cloud Audit Logs record your users and service accounts.
Flow logs describe network traffic; they do not record which principal called an API.
A request count metric shows call volume, not who made each call.

services.name: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
patterns: Vertex AI(?! Search| Pipelines| Agent Builder)
services.what: Agent Platform is Google Cloud's platform to build, deploy, govern, and optimize agents and model-based solutions. It hosts Gemini and more than 200 foundation models, plus managed training, pipelines, endpoints, and monitoring.
cues: A team calls a Google-managed Gemini model, and ML processing must stay in the EU.
Developers must build, deploy, and govern custom agents for production.
A data science team wants shared notebooks with IAM access and no VMs to manage.
The team wants managed training, model versions, endpoints, and monitoring in one platform.
traps: The global endpoint gives no data residency guarantee; use a regional or a US or EU multi-region endpoint.
Prediction calls do not appear in Admin Activity logs; enable Data Access audit logs for the Agent Platform API.

confused.tell: Developers build and govern agents on Agent Platform; employees find and use them in the Gemini Enterprise app.
A standard Agent Platform deployment keeps at least one replica; a Cloud Run GPU service scales to zero for bursty traffic.
GKE gives deep control and portability, but you operate Kubernetes; Agent Platform fits teams that want no infrastructure.

services.name: Gemini models
services.what: Gemini is Google's family of multimodal foundation models on Agent Platform. It reads text, images, audio, and video, and it comes in Pro, Flash, and Flash-Lite tiers.
cues: One summary must reflect both what people say and what appears on screen in a video.
Output must follow a fixed catalog schema or a list of allowed values.
Content moderation needs a custom policy with exceptions, and moderators must see the reasoning.
A large backlog, such as a whole product catalog, needs generation with no real-time need.
traps: Tuning teaches a skill, not facts, so documents that change every week belong in grounding, not in tuning jobs.
A tuned model does not carry over to a new Gemini version; you run a new tuning job.

confused.tell: Video Intelligence is deprecated, and its label and explicit content detection read only pictures; Gemini summarizes video with its audio in one request.
Vision API returns generic labels; Gemini with a response schema returns your own attributes from text and images together.
AutoML needs labeled data and training for image or tabular data; Gemini needs only a prompt.

services.name: Model Garden
services.what: Model Garden is a library to discover, test, customize, and deploy Google, partner, and open models. Partner models such as Anthropic Claude run as a managed API. You can self-deploy open models to your own endpoint.
cues: The team has custom fine-tuned weights for an open model and needs a dedicated endpoint in a chosen region.
Rules forbid sending data to a multi-tenant managed service.
A data science team wants to call a partner model, such as Anthropic Claude, as a managed API.
An organization must control which models people can use, tune, or deploy.
traps: Model as a Service is multi-tenant and serves base models, so custom weights or a multi-tenant ban call for self-deployment.
The vertexai.allowedModels policy covers Model Garden models only, not models in Model Registry.

confused.tell: A Gemini batch job needs no endpoint; a self-deployed Model Garden model means you deploy, scale, and pay for the endpoint.
Deploy a Hugging Face model on Agent Platform for managed MLOps, or on GKE for Kubernetes skills and fine control.
Model Garden offers Google, partner, and open models; Model Registry lists your own model versions.

services.name: Agent Builder (ADK and Agent Runtime)
services.what: Agent Builder is the exam guide name for the agent tools in Agent Platform. Developers write agents in code with the Agent Development Kit (ADK). Agent Runtime runs them in production as a fully managed runtime.
cues: Developers built an agent with ADK and want managed deployment and scaling with no servers or clusters.
Developers write a multi-agent system in Python, TypeScript, Go, or Java.
An agent must remember users across sessions, not only within one conversation.
traps: Older questions can use Agent Builder to mean Agent Search, so search over company content points to Agent Search.
Agent Platform Pipelines orchestrates ML workflows; it does not serve an interactive agent.

confused.tell: ADK is a code-based framework that needs developers; CX Agent Studio is minimal-code for customer conversations.
Workflow Builder in Gemini Enterprise is a no-code tool for employee agents; it does not host ADK code.
GKE can host an ADK agent, but the team operates the cluster; Agent Runtime is fully managed.

services.name: Agent Search
services.what: Agent Search is a Google-quality search engine over your data for search, recommendation, and RAG apps. It gives AI answers grounded in your data, with citations.
cues: A Gemini assistant invents answers about private policy files in Cloud Storage that change every week.
A media company wants personalized watch-next recommendations from its user events, with little ML experience.
The team wants search over its own content with the least build work.
Clinicians need search over healthcare records in FHIR data stores.
traps: A website app covers only the sites that you index, not internal systems or the current public web.

confused.tell: Agent Search is an out-of-the-box search engine; RAG Engine lets you control the RAG pipeline without operating each part.
Gemini Enterprise is a ready employee app with prebuilt connectors to Jira or SharePoint; Agent Search is what you build search apps on.
Product search and recommendations for a retailer point to AI Commerce Search, not Agent Search custom search.

services.name: RAG Engine and Vector Search
services.what: RAG Engine is a managed RAG framework that ingests, chunks, embeds, indexes, and retrieves your data in a corpus. Vector Search is an approximate nearest neighbor engine for your own embeddings that scales to billions of vectors.
cues: The team wants to control the RAG pipeline but not operate each part.
A Gemini app must retrieve current passages from private files at request time.
The team builds its own retrieval or semantic search with its own embeddings.
traps: RAG Engine supports VPC Service Controls and CMEK but not data residency, so it fails a mandatory residency rule.
A weekly job that downloads web pages into a corpus is not current web information; use web grounding instead.

confused.tell: Agent Search gives Google-quality search with the least build work; RAG Engine gives more control of each RAG stage.
Vector Search can power product search, but you then build ranking and personalization yourself.
Feature Store serves features for training and serving; for embeddings, Google points to Vector Search.

services.name: Agent Platform Pipelines
services.what: Agent Platform Pipelines runs ML workflows as a graph of container steps, with no cluster to manage. Each run records its parameters and artifacts in ML Metadata, which gives lineage for audits.
cues: An ML workflow is container-based and runs entirely inside Agent Platform.
The model must retrain on a schedule or when new training data arrives.
Auditors need to trace what each training run consumed and produced.
traps: Use the KFP SDK for most pipelines; choose TFX only for terabytes of structured or text data with TensorFlow.
Runs default to the Compute Engine default service account; the recommended answer is a dedicated service account with granular permissions.

confused.tell: Choose Managed Service for Apache Airflow when the flow spans unrelated systems, such as on-premises databases, Spark, and partner APIs.
Pipelines orchestrates ML workflows; an interactive agent runs on Agent Runtime.
A Cloud Run function is event-driven glue that starts a pipeline run; it is not the place to train.

services.name: Model Registry, Model Monitoring, and Feature Store
services.what: Model Registry versions and deploys models, and Model Monitoring watches tabular model inputs for skew and drift. Feature Store gives the same features to training and online serving, which avoids training-serving skew.
cues: The team has the original training data and wants alerts when production inputs differ from it.
The training data is not available, and the team wants alerts when inputs change over time.
The team wants a movable alias to deploy or roll back a specific model version.
Experiments, training, and online serving must all use the same feature values.
traps: Model Monitoring tracks drift over time; it does not explain why the model gave one prediction its score.
Vertex Explainable AI is deprecated, so do not design around it; Google suggests open-source SHAP or LIME.

confused.tell: Cloud Monitoring alerts on latency and errors; Model Monitoring alerts on changes in feature values.
Data Access audit logs record who called a prediction endpoint; Model Monitoring does not.

services.name: AutoML
services.what: AutoML trains models on Agent Platform with little code, for image and tabular data only. It requires a managed dataset.
cues: A team needs a custom image model, such as object detection, with little code.
A tabular prediction problem fits AutoML, and the team wants little code.
traps: AutoML Text and AutoML Video are shut down, so prompt or tune a Gemini model for text or video.
AutoML image models ignore accompanying text, so a task that mixes text and images fits a Gemini prompt.

confused.tell: If a prompt meets the need with no training, Gemini is the lower-effort answer; AutoML needs labeled data and training.
When all data is in BigQuery and the team knows SQL, BigQuery ML trains without moving data.

docs.title: Train and use your own models

services.name: BigQuery ML
services.what: BigQuery ML lets SQL users create and run models inside BigQuery. It can also call Agent Platform models from SQL, so the data stays in the warehouse.
cues: All the data is in BigQuery, and the analysts know SQL but not Python.
BigQuery ML supports the needed model type, and the team wants to avoid moving data.
Analysts want forecasts in SQL without creating or managing a model.
Analysts want LLM results over warehouse data from SQL.
traps: BigQuery ML supports only batch predictions; for online predictions, register the model in Model Registry and deploy it to an endpoint.
ARIMA_PLUS requires a model that you create and manage; AI.FORECAST with the built-in TimesFM model does not.

confused.tell: Agent Platform custom training reads data out of BigQuery and needs ML code; BigQuery ML keeps the work in SQL in the warehouse.

services.name: AI Hypercomputer (GPUs, TPUs, Dynamic Workload Scheduler)
services.what: AI Hypercomputer is Google Cloud's integrated system of GPUs, TPUs, networking, storage, open software, and consumption options. You do not buy it as one product; you use its parts through Compute Engine, GKE, and Agent Platform.
cues: A GPU job runs up to seven days, can wait for capacity, and cannot be preempted.
A training run must start on a fixed date and last 1 to 90 days.
Training on clustered GPUs lasts months and must start on a known date up to one year ahead.
Matrix math dominates the model, and the training loop has no custom operations.
traps: Flex-start is best effort and lasts at most seven days, so it cannot assure a fixed-date or multi-week run.
Calendar mode lasts at most 90 days, and GPU requests start at least 87 hours after you submit them.

confused.tell: Spot VMs have the deepest discount but can be preempted at any time; Flex-start VMs are not preempted.
An on-demand reservation bills from the time you create it; a calendar-mode future reservation starts on the date you choose.
Cloud Run GPUs fit smaller models that scale to zero with no reservation, but allow one GPU per instance.

services.aws: Amazon EC2 Trn1, Inf1, and P5 instances (for Cloud TPUs and GPUs)

services.name: Gemini Enterprise
patterns: Gemini Enterprise(?! Agent Platform| for Customer)
services.what: Gemini Enterprise is an intranet search, AI assistant, and agentic platform for employees. Prebuilt connectors reach systems such as Confluence, Jira, SharePoint, and ServiceNow, and results follow each user's permissions.
cues: Employees lose time searching Confluence, Jira, SharePoint, and ServiceNow and want one AI assistant.
Search results must include only documents that each employee can already open.
Business users want to build their own agents with no code.
Developers built ADK agents, and employees must find and run them in one place.
traps: Gemini Enterprise is not the developer platform; developers build and govern custom agents on Agent Platform.
CMEK needs a US or EU multi-region app or data store, not a global one.

confused.tell: Gemini Notebook Enterprise fits a known set of trusted sources; Gemini Enterprise fits search where the starting place is unknown.
A custom RAG app on Agent Platform needs connector code and permission checks; Gemini Enterprise has them prebuilt.
Workflow Builder makes agents for employees; customer-facing call and chat agents belong in CX Agent Studio.

services.name: Gemini Notebook Enterprise
services.what: Gemini Notebook Enterprise is a highly compliant, enterprise version of Gemini Notebook. It builds a reference point for a topic from known, trusted sources that users add.
cues: A small team analyzes a fixed set of documents and shares its findings with a few colleagues.
Source data must stay in the US or EU multi-region.
Company policy forbids public sharing links, so access must go through IAM roles.
traps: Copying all company documents into notebooks each month leaves stale copies that lose their source permissions.
Projects inside a VPC Service Controls perimeter cannot add website URLs as notebook sources.

confused.tell: Gemini Enterprise connects to many company systems with permission-aware search; a notebook uses only the sources that users add.
A custom RAG app on Agent Platform needs development work that the notebook product already covers.

services.name: CX Agent Studio (Gemini Enterprise for Customer Experience)
services.what: CX Agent Studio is a minimal-code builder for conversational agents in Gemini Enterprise for Customer Experience (GECX), built on ADK. It is the evolution of Dialogflow CX, and agents can be generative, deterministic, or both.
cues: A support team, not developers, builds a 24/7 agent that answers open questions and follows fixed steps for account tasks.
A retailer replaces its IVR with virtual agents that answer and route phone calls.
Routine calls and orders must move from human agents to a virtual agent on a Google Telephony Platform number.
Customers tell the agent phone numbers and addresses that must never reach stored history or logs.
traps: Dialogflow ES and CX are legacy, so do not pick them for a new generative agent.
CMEK and VPC Service Controls do not remove sensitive values from stored conversations; enable redaction with a Sensitive Data Protection template.

confused.tell: ADK on Agent Runtime is code-first and needs developers; CX Agent Studio is minimal-code.
Workflow Builder in Gemini Enterprise makes employee agents, not customer-facing call agents.
Speech-to-Text transcripts help later analysis but handle no calls; a CX Agent Studio agent takes routine calls itself.

services.aws: Amazon Lex (GECX as a whole maps to Amazon Connect)

services.name: AI Commerce Search
services.what: AI Commerce Search gives retailers product search and recommendations, as part of GECX. Google handles model training, tuning, and infrastructure, and ranking uses the catalog and real-time user events.
cues: A retailer wants better product discoverability and conversion but will not build, train, or tune ranking models.
The Cymbal case asks for Google Cloud's Discovery AI to find the most relevant products.
Shoppers describe what they need in natural language and answer follow-up questions.
The catalog uses custom key/value attributes and changes every week.
traps: The Merchant Center connector is deprecated for new customers; import through BigQuery or the Catalog API.
A one-time catalog import goes stale; schedule regular imports, ideally daily.

confused.tell: Agent Search custom search covers any industry's content; retail product search with catalog, events, and conversion ranking is AI Commerce Search.
Vector Search can power semantic product search, but you then build ranking and personalization yourself.
An agent that generates SQL still searches the relational tables; the Conversational agent in AI Commerce Search uses the catalog and ranking.

services.name: Cloud Vision API
services.what: Cloud Vision API is a pre-trained API that analyzes images. It returns labels, faces, landmarks, text, and SafeSearch ratings for explicit content.
cues: The first release must flag explicit uploaded images with a pre-trained API and no training.
The app needs fast text extraction from images at high volume.
The app needs labels, landmarks, or face detection for still images.
traps: Face detection finds faces but does not identify people.
Vision OCR is the wrong choice for a scanned-document pipeline; Google recommends Document AI there.

confused.tell: Vision text detection returns raw text; Document AI keeps form structure, such as tables and key-value pairs, in a pipeline.
Vision returns generic labels and cannot edit images; Gemini returns your own schema and edits images over several turns.

services.name: Video Intelligence API
services.what: The Video Intelligence API is a pre-trained video analysis API. It is deprecated from September 14, 2026 and shuts down on September 14, 2027, and Google recommends Gemini models instead.
cues: An option offers label, shot, or explicit content detection on video: check whether the design must stay supported for years.
An existing design uses the API, and the question asks for its supported replacement.
traps: Choosing it for a new design ignores its deprecation; Google recommends Gemini video understanding.
Explicit content detection checks frames for adult content only, so it misses spoken hate speech and custom exceptions.

confused.tell: Gemini reads video with its audio and returns metadata and summaries in one request.
Vision API handles still images; Video Intelligence handles video but is deprecated.

services.name: Speech-to-Text and Text-to-Speech
services.what: Speech-to-Text is a pre-trained API that transcribes audio with synchronous, batch, or streaming recognition. Text-to-Speech turns text into spoken audio.
cues: Long recordings in Cloud Storage, up to 480 minutes, need transcripts but no real-time answer.
Live audio must be transcribed as it arrives.
Phone call audio at 8 kHz, for example from an IVR, needs transcription.
Audio must be processed in a specific region, such as Belgium.
traps: Synchronous recognition accepts only 1 minute of audio or less.
Chirp 3 transcription works only in the Speech-to-Text V2 API, not V1.

confused.tell: A transcript loses what appears on screen; Gemini summarizes video with its audio in one request.
The Agent Platform speech feature accepts at most 60 seconds or 10 MB; long files need Speech-to-Text batch recognition.
Transcripts handle no calls; a CX Agent Studio agent automates routine calls.

services.name: Natural Language API
services.what: The Natural Language API is a pre-trained API for text. It returns sentiment, entities, and entity sentiment, and it moderates text against safety attributes.
cues: User comments must be flagged for harmful content with a pre-trained API and no training.
The app needs sentiment or named entities from text.
traps: Sentiment shows opinion, not harm; a negative review is not harmful content.
Moderating a video transcript sees only the words, so it misses on-screen content.

confused.tell: Entity analysis cannot limit results to your catalog values; Gemini with a response schema can.
Entity analysis reads text but cannot read scanned pages or keep table structure.
Entity analysis does not control how terms translate; a Translation Advanced glossary does.

services.name: Cloud Translation
services.what: Cloud Translation is a pre-trained translation API with Basic and Advanced editions. Advanced adds glossaries and regional endpoints, such as the EU.
cues: Product names and regulated terms must translate the same way every time.
Translation requests must be processed in the EU.
The app translates casual user content, such as chat or comments, with an API key.
traps: Translation - Advanced does not accept API keys.
Basic has no glossaries, and the global endpoint does not keep processing in the EU.

confused.tell: Entity analysis finds terms but does not control how they translate; an Advanced glossary does.
Model Garden translation models fit only when you build your own end-to-end translation MLOps pipeline.

docs.title: Overview of the Cloud Translation API

services.name: Document AI
services.what: Document AI is a service for document processing pipelines and scanned documents. Its processors extract text, form tables, key-value pairs, RAG chunks, and fields from known or custom document types.
cues: Thousands of scanned claim forms arrive as PDFs and must flow into a system through an automated pipeline.
The pipeline must extract tables and key-value pairs from forms.
Documents must be split into chunks for a RAG index.
Fields must come from the company's own document type, without training a model.
traps: The Gemini-based v1.6 processor versions (Preview) use the global endpoint, so they do not meet data residency rules.

confused.tell: Vision text detection returns raw text from images; Document AI keeps form structure in a pipeline.
Entity analysis finds entities in text but cannot read scanned pages or keep tables.

services.name: Cloud Build
services.what: Cloud Build runs the CI stage on Google Cloud: build, test, and scan steps that start from triggers. It pushes images to Artifact Registry and can create a Cloud Deploy release.
cues: Builds must start on each push or pull request, and tests must gate the merge.
Builds must reach a server that has only a private IP address.
Auditors need proof that the company's pipeline built each image from its own repository.
Images with critical vulnerabilities must never reach the registry.
traps: Cloud Build creates no provenance when a docker push step pushes the image, so list it in the images field.
Triggers and worker pools are not replicated across regions, so prepare disabled triggers and pools in a second region.

confused.tell: A Cloud Build approval gates the build, while Cloud Deploy approvals gate the rollout to a target.
Automatic scanning only reports after the push, while On-Demand Scanning in the build can fail it.
Cloud Build signs attestations at build time, and Binary Authorization checks them when an image deploys.

services.name: Artifact Registry
services.what: Artifact Registry stores container images and language packages in one service. Each repository has a mode, such as standard, remote, or virtual, that you cannot change later.
cues: Builds fail when Docker Hub or another upstream source has an outage.
An attacker can publish a public package with the same name as an internal package.
A regional registry outage must not stop deployments or GKE scale-out.
Teams need one location to store and scan the container images for all clusters.
traps: A tag is a movable label, so it proves nothing about how an image was built; deploy by digest.
An Artifact Registry repository is not a Git service, and it has no pull requests.

confused.tell: Artifact Registry stores the artifacts, and Artifact Analysis scans them and only reports vulnerabilities.
Binary Authorization controls which images deploy to GKE or Cloud Run, not which packages a build downloads.
A bucket of image tarballs is not a container registry, so clusters cannot pull images from it.

services.name: Cloud Deploy
services.what: Cloud Deploy is a managed continuous delivery service. It promotes one release through a sequence of GKE or Cloud Run targets, with approvals, canary rollouts, and rollback.
cues: Each release must move through test, staging, and production in a defined order.
In production, a new version must reach a small share of users first.
A release manager must approve each production rollout in a ticketing system such as ServiceNow.
No production deployment may start during a seasonal change freeze.
traps: The first rollout to a new target skips the canary phases and deploys to 100% of traffic.
Cloud Deploy does not replicate releases across regions, so keep pipeline and target definitions in source control.

confused.tell: Cloud Build builds and tests the image, and Cloud Deploy promotes the release and rolls it back.
If no user may see the new backend yet, mirror requests at the load balancer instead of a canary.
Cloud Deploy delivers application releases, while Application Design Center gives governed infrastructure templates.

services.name: Terraform and Infrastructure Manager
services.what: Terraform is Google's recommended IaC tool for Google Cloud. Infrastructure Manager runs Terraform for you in Cloud Build and stores the state, logs, and configuration of each revision.
cues: Several engineers run Terraform against one project, and their local state files conflict.
The team wants Google to run Terraform and keep the state, instead of a self-managed pipeline.
The DR environment must exist only during a failover, to avoid idle infrastructure.
Deployment Manager configurations must move to a Google-managed IaC service.
traps: An Infrastructure Manager configuration must not define a backend block, because the service manages the state.
Authoritative IAM resources such as google_project_iam_policy can remove Google-managed roles, so use google_*_iam_member resources.

confused.tell: Terraform finds drift only when you run it, while Config Connector reconciles resources continuously.
Infrastructure Manager provisions infrastructure and does not deploy applications, which is Cloud Deploy's job.
Deployment Manager lost support on April 1, 2026, so new IaC work uses Terraform or Infrastructure Manager.

services.name: Deployment Manager
services.what: Deployment Manager is Google's former IaC service, with YAML configurations and Jinja or Python templates. Support stopped on April 1, 2026, and Google turns it down after June 30, 2027.
cues: A company still manages its projects with Deployment Manager YAML configurations and Jinja templates.
The team must keep those resources under IaC with the least rewrite effort.
traps: Keeping Deployment Manager and opening support cases fails, because Google rejects standard support tickets.
Infrastructure Manager has no Deployment Manager-style rollback, so you deploy the previous configuration as a new revision.

confused.tell: The migration path is DM Convert to Terraform, then an import into Infrastructure Manager.
Bulk export to Config Connector on your own cluster is not a managed Terraform service or the migration path.

services.name: Config Connector
services.what: Config Connector is an open source Kubernetes add-on whose custom resources and controllers create and manage Google Cloud resources. Config Controller is its hosted version, with Config Sync and Policy Controller.
cues: Teams that work in Kubernetes with GitOps want to request Cloud SQL or Pub/Sub as Kubernetes resources.
Changes made in the console must be reverted automatically.
The platform team does not want to install or upgrade the controllers.
traps: The add-on on your own GKE cluster leaves installs and upgrades to you, and it gives no policy enforcement.
Config Connector changes resources with its own service account, so apply its objects only from a trusted repository.

confused.tell: Terraform shows a change in a plan before it happens, while Config Connector corrects drift at each reconciliation.
Config Connector creates cloud resources, and Policy Controller blocks noncompliant resources before they are created.

services.name: Policy Controller
services.what: Policy Controller enforces programmable policies in GKE clusters, as admission control and audit. It is based on Open Policy Agent Gatekeeper and has prebuilt policy bundles.
cues: Noncompliant Kubernetes changes must be blocked on every cluster in a fleet.
Past outages came from misconfigured clusters, and the company wants guardrails instead of manual reviews.
Policy violations must be blocked before GitOps creates cloud resources in Config Controller.
traps: A nightly kubectl script or a weekly review does not block changes, and drift between runs stays.

confused.tell: Organization Policy custom constraints check Google Cloud API calls, while Policy Controller checks objects in the cluster.
Binary Authorization decides which images may deploy, while Policy Controller denies noncompliant configurations.

services.aws: OPA Gatekeeper that you run on Amazon EKS

services.name: App Hub and Application Design Center
services.what: App Hub groups existing services and workloads from many projects into applications, with owners, criticality, and environment. Application Design Center lets platform teams publish approved templates that developers deploy.
cues: Developers must deploy new applications by themselves from approved templates with standards built in.
Each deployed application must appear in App Hub automatically.
One Gemini Cloud Assist investigation must cover resources in three separate projects.
Designs must pass a Security Command Center policy check and go out as Terraform through the existing pipeline.
traps: App Hub does not deploy new applications, because it organizes resources that already exist.
Gemini Cloud Assist does not support applications in a single-project boundary, so use an app-enabled folder.

confused.tell: Cloud Deploy delivers releases to targets, and Application Design Center deploys governed infrastructure templates.
Gemini Cloud Assist drafts designs and runs investigations, and App Hub supplies the cross-project application boundary.

services.aws: AWS Service Catalog (for Application Design Center)

services.name: Cloud Shell and Cloud Code
services.what: Cloud Shell gives each user a browser terminal on a temporary VM that Google owns and keeps up to date. Cloud Code adds IDE support for Kubernetes and Cloud Run apps, including in Cloud Shell Editor.
cues: An administrator needs quick, interactive command-line access from a browser.
A tool that the team installs with apt-get is missing in each new session.
Developers want to build and debug Kubernetes or Cloud Run apps in VS Code or IntelliJ.
traps: A nightly or multi-hour job in Cloud Shell fails, because non-interactive sessions end after 40 minutes.
Ephemeral mode has no persistent disk, so all files are lost at session end.

confused.tell: Cloud Shell is for people, while scheduled automation runs gcloud or client libraries with a service account identity.

services.name: Google Cloud CLI, client libraries, and emulators
services.what: Scripts use the gcloud CLI and bq, code uses the Cloud Client Libraries, and emulators support local tests. Client libraries find credentials through Application Default Credentials (ADC).
cues: Developers must test locally with exactly a service account's permissions, and key creation is blocked.
CI needs fast integration tests against Spanner, Pub/Sub, Firestore, or Bigtable with no cloud cost.
Backup scripts use gsutil and must now manage soft-deleted objects.
Automation scripts parse the default gcloud table output, which can change in a later release.
traps: gcloud auth login gives credentials only to the gcloud CLI, so run gcloud auth application-default login for client libraries.
The Spanner emulator supports no IAM and has no comparable performance, so test access and latency on a real instance.

confused.tell: A service account key is the last resort, and impersonation through ADC gives short-lived credentials instead.
From on-premises, use gcloud storage below 1 TB, and Storage Transfer Service or Transfer Appliance above 1 TB.

services.aws: AWS SDKs (for Cloud Client Libraries) and the SDK default credential chain (for ADC)

services.name: Cloud Monitoring
services.what: Cloud Monitoring collects metrics and runs dashboards, uptime checks, synthetic monitors, SLOs, and alerting policies. It is on by default in each project and collects metrics for most Google Cloud services.
cues: One SRE team needs dashboards and alerting policies across many projects.
VM memory charts are empty because the VMs have no Ops Agent.
Teams want to keep PromQL alerts and Grafana dashboards but stop running Prometheus servers.
The team must learn that checkout is broken before customers report it.
traps: A production project as the scoping project forces filters on its own charts and alerts, so use a project without resources.
Paging on high CPU alerts on a cause, so page on user-visible symptoms or SLO burn rate instead.

confused.tell: Log sinks centralize logs, not metrics, while a metrics scope gives one view of metrics across projects.
Model Monitoring detects skew or drift in feature values, while Cloud Monitoring alerts on endpoint latency and errors.

services.name: Cloud Logging and Observability Analytics
services.what: Cloud Logging stores, searches, and routes log entries. Every entry passes the Log Router, whose sinks send it to log buckets, BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub, or another project.
cues: Compliance requires logs from many projects in one central bucket with custom retention.
A one-time analysis must count stored log entries per customer per hour with SQL.
Most log volume is successful health checks that nobody reads, and the bill must drop.
Audit logs must be kept for seven years at the lowest cost.
traps: A new sink or log-based metric does not cover old entries, so copy old logs from the bucket or query them in Observability Analytics.
Exclusion filters cut storage cost but not entries.write API calls or quota.

confused.tell: Admin Activity logs are always written to the _Required bucket, while Data Access logs are off by default except some BigQuery services.
A sink to BigQuery routes only new entries, while Observability Analytics queries logs that are already stored.
Cloud Logging answers what happened in detail, while Cloud Monitoring tracks metrics, SLOs, and alerts.

services.aws: CloudWatch Logs, with Observability Analytics as the CloudWatch Logs Insights equivalent

services.name: Cloud Trace, Cloud Profiler, and Error Reporting
services.what: Cloud Trace follows one request across services to show where latency comes from. Cloud Profiler shows which code uses CPU and memory in production, and Error Reporting groups error events by root cause.
cues: CPU use rose after a release, but latency and error rates did not change.
One service in a call chain adds latency, and the team must find which one.
The team wants to know which exceptions are new since the last release.
traps: Cloud Trace cannot find a CPU hot spot, because it shows latency between services, not CPU use in methods.
Error Reporting does not analyze log entries in CMEK-enabled log buckets.

confused.tell: Error Reporting groups application errors, while Admin Activity audit logs show who changed a configuration.
Cloud Trace measures request latency in instrumented code, while Connectivity Tests checks firewall rules and routes.

services.aws: AWS X-Ray (Cloud Trace) and Amazon CodeGuru Profiler (Cloud Profiler)

services.name: VPC Flow Logs
services.what: VPC Flow Logs record sampled 5-tuple flow records for a network, subnet, VLAN attachment, or VPN tunnel. Use them for network monitoring, forensics, and cost analysis.
cues: The security team needs flow records for forensics after a breach.
The network team needs flow data for monitoring or cost analysis.
Operators want to see which flows carry their traffic without writing SQL queries.
traps: Flow logs record past traffic, so they cannot check a new firewall policy before it carries traffic.

confused.tell: To prove what one firewall rule denied, use firewall rules logging, because flow logs miss denied ingress packets.
Packet Mirroring copies full packets with payloads, while flow logs hold only sampled connection data.
Flow logs describe network traffic and never record which principal called an API or changed a rule.

services.name: Gemini Cloud Assist
services.what: Gemini Cloud Assist is an AI assistant (Preview) for design, operations, troubleshooting, and cost work in Google Cloud. It has the same permissions as the user who asks it.
cues: Operators want chat help to list resources, IAM grants, or recent changes in a project without residency rules.
Application teams want to turn natural-language requirements into Terraform in Application Design Center.
An SRE team with Premium Support wants ranked root-cause hypotheses from logs, metrics, and configuration.
traps: Do not enable it in projects with data residency or CMEK rules, because it can store data in any data center.
Investigations need a Premium Support contract or account-team access since April 10, 2026.

confused.tell: A VPC Service Controls perimeter limits what the assistant can reach, but it adds no data residency or CMEK.
Active Assist produces recommendations by value category, while Gemini Cloud Assist is a chat assistant with agents.
An investigation covers one project or one App Hub application, so group cross-project resources in App Hub.

services.aws: Amazon Q Developer in the AWS console

services.name: Active Assist and Recommender
services.what: Active Assist is the portfolio of Google Cloud tools, including Recommender, that give recommendations and insights. Each recommender belongs to a value category such as cost, security, performance, reliability, or manageability.
cues: The company wants to find idle VMs, idle disks, or oversized machine types.
The security team wants to remove excess IAM permissions or reclaim unattended projects.
Finance wants a committed use discount amount based on recent usage.
traps: Applying recommendations automatically is risky, so a qualified reviewer assesses each one, or you set up rollback first.
The machine type recommender uses only 8 days of data, so it can miss a monthly peak.

confused.tell: Migration Center discovers assets before a move, while Active Assist recommends changes to existing Google Cloud resources.
Recommenders list specific changes to review, while Gemini Cloud Assist chat summarizes cost drivers and waste.

services.name: VM Manager
services.what: VM Manager is a Compute Engine suite with three services: Patch, OS inventory management, and OS policies. It needs the OS Config API, and each VM needs an active OS Config agent and an attached service account.
cues: Hundreds of VMs need monthly OS patches in a window, with a limit on VMs disrupted per zone.
Operations needs patch compliance reports and a list of installed packages and available updates.
Agents and baseline packages must stay in a declared state across a VM fleet.
traps: An OS policy with a fixed package list keeps a state but does not schedule patching or limit disruption.
Patching fails on VMs without an attached service account or without a route to their package repositories.

confused.tell: Patch jobs skip MIG VMs by default, and a MIG changes through a new instance template and a rolling update.
A scheduled function that runs updates over SSH is custom code, while a patch deployment is a managed feature.

services.name: Cloud Customer Care
services.what: Cloud Customer Care is Google Cloud's support offering, with four services: Basic, Standard, Enhanced, and Premium. The service applies to all projects in the organization, and only an Organization Administrator can change it.
cues: Critical production cases need a first response within 15 minutes and an assigned technical contact.
Production workloads need a 1-hour response for critical issues, 24/7.
A production outage got worse after someone opened the case at P3.
A launch or a sale causes a short traffic peak that needs extra support.
traps: Escalation flags a broken support process and does not speed up a case, so raise the priority instead.
Enhanced Support includes no Technical Account Manager, because only Premium Support includes one.

confused.tell: Check Personalized Service Health for Google incidents, and do not open cases that duplicate a known issue.

docs.title: Get support with Cloud Customer Care

services.name: Personalized Service Health
services.what: Personalized Service Health (PSH) is the primary source for Google Cloud incidents that affect your projects, including limited-scope ones. It offers a console dashboard, an API, log-based alerts, and organization views.
cues: The public status page shows no incidents, but one zone seems to fail.
The SRE team wants Google Cloud incident data in its process without paging on every event.
Operators need one view of Google Cloud incidents for all projects in the organization.
traps: A green public status page proves nothing, because it shows only broad, severe incidents.
PSH depends on core services such as IAM, so plan a fallback to the public status page and its RSS feed.

confused.tell: PSH shows whether a Google incident affects your projects, so check it before you open a case that duplicates a known issue.

services.name: Migration Center
services.what: Migration Center is a platform for asset discovery, assessment, planning, and cost estimates. It groups assets and generates TCO reports from your migration preferences.
cues: The CFO wants a TCO estimate for each application, based on the real VM sizes.
Security allows no new software in the data center, but the team has RVTools or CSV exports to import.
The team must compare on-demand, commitment, license, and tenancy scenarios side by side before the move.
traps: The default pricing track, No preference, means a 3-year resource-based CUD, not on-demand prices.
You choose the data region once at activation, and a preference set's Location only sets where migrated VMs run.

confused.tell: Migration Center discovers assets and estimates cost, while Migrate to Virtual Machines moves the VMs.
Active Assist recommends changes to resources already on Google Cloud, while Migration Center assesses the source environment before the move.

services.name: Migrate to Virtual Machines
services.what: Migrate to Virtual Machines is a lift-and-shift tool. It moves VMs from vSphere, AWS, Azure, and VMware Engine to Compute Engine. It replicates disks while the source runs, supports test clones, and needs a short cutover.
cues: The company wants to rehost VMs on Compute Engine now and adopt managed services later.
The team must test a migrated VM in an isolated sandbox while the source VM keeps running.
Virtual disk images such as VMDK or VHD must become Compute Engine images.
traps: Rollback is manual, and data written to the new VM is not copied back to the source.
Moving database or cache servers as VMs keeps the patching and operations work, so it misses a managed-service goal.

confused.tell: If the team must keep vCenter, NSX, and VMware processes, or needs live migration, use VMware Engine with HCX.
Migrate to Containers moves applications into containers on GKE or Cloud Run. Migrate to Virtual Machines keeps them as VMs.
Database Migration Service moves databases into managed Cloud SQL or AlloyDB, while Migrate to Virtual Machines moves whole servers.

services.name: Migrate to Containers
services.what: Migrate to Containers moves workloads from VMs into containers on GKE, GKE Autopilot, or Cloud Run. It fits web and application servers such as Tomcat, JBoss, WebSphere, and IIS.
cues: Web or application servers on VMs must be replatformed into containers on GKE or Cloud Run.
Multi-tier stacks such as LAMP, or low duty-cycle test and training labs, should run as containers.
traps: Large in-memory databases, kernel-mode drivers, and licenses tied to hardware IDs are not a good fit.
Containerizing hundreds of VMs is a modernization project, so it does not fit a short exit deadline.

confused.tell: Migrate to Virtual Machines rehosts VMs on Compute Engine without containerizing them.
A fast data center exit that keeps VMware tools and runbooks fits VMware Engine, not containerization.

services.name: Database Migration Service
services.what: Database Migration Service migrates MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, and Oracle databases into Cloud SQL or AlloyDB for PostgreSQL. Continuous migrations replicate changes until cutover, for minimal downtime.
cues: Self-managed MySQL or SQL Server must move to the same engine on Cloud SQL with small code changes.
A database must move to a new primary on Cloud SQL or AlloyDB with minimal downtime.
Oracle or SQL Server must convert to PostgreSQL, with schema and code conversion in a conversion workspace.
